bio.en: Mihika Kapoor is a product manager at Figma renowned for creating a compelling vision and getting teams to see it, and a repeated "best PM" cited by peers.
bio.zh: 米希卡·卡普尔（Mihika Kapoor）是 Figma 的产品经理，以"能创造令人信服的愿景、并让团队看见它"而闻名，被同行多次评为"最佳 PM"。

summary.en: Mihika argues a PM's scope should be the whole world, with nothing off-limits, and that prototyping before a project is greenlit builds shared vision. She shares Figma's "Maker Week" hackathon as a way to give people space for wildly ambitious ideas. The episode is a master class in vision-setting and entrepreneurial culture.
summary.zh: 米希卡认为，PM 的视野应当是"全世界"，没有什么是禁区；在项目获批前就做设计与原型，能建立共同愿景。她分享了 Figma 的 "Maker Week" 内部黑客松，作为给员工空间去追求狂野想法的做法。本期是关于"设定愿景与创业文化"的大师课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I asked on Twitter, "Who's the best product manager you've worked with?" You were the most mentioned.
turns.zh: 我在 Twitter 上问了大家："你共事过最优秀的产品经理是谁？" 被提到次数最多的人就是你。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: My take is that your scope is the world. Nothing should ever perceive as being out of bounds.
turns.zh: 我的观点是，你的视野范围就是整个世界。任何事都不应该让人觉得"这超出了我的边界"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: VP of product at Figma told me, "Mahika is really great at creating a vision and getting people to see what she sees."
turns.zh: Figma 的产品副总裁告诉我："Mahika 非常擅长构建愿景，并让其他人看到她所看到的东西。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: We lean heavily into designing and prototyping even before a project gets a green light. If you and your team do your job correctly, what does the world look like?
turns.zh: 我们会在项目甚至还没获得绿灯批准之前，就大量投入设计和原型制作。如果你和你的团队把工作做到位，那么世界会是什么样子？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Say somebody wants to make their culture more entrepreneurial, what does it take?
turns.zh: 假设有人想让自己的团队文化更有创业精神，这都需要什么？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: We have this concept called Maker Week, which is our internal hackathon, giving people the breathing space to see ahead into the horizon and be wildly ambitious.
turns.zh: 我们有一个叫 Maker Week 的概念，这是我们内部的黑客马拉松，给大家留出喘息的空间，去眺望地平线、去大胆地怀抱野心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, my guest is Mahika Kapoor. Mahika is a design engineering PM hybrid at Figma, where she was an early PM on FigJam, and is now spearheading development of a new product that the company's going to launch in June. She's known as the go-to person at Figma for leading new zero-to-one products. And as you'll hear in our conversation, is beloved by everybody that works with her. Prior to Figma, Mahika founded Design Nation, a national nonprofit that democratizes undergraduate student access to a design education, and led several products and launches at Meta, focused on commerce and creators.
turns.zh: 今天的嘉宾是 Mahika Kapoor。Mahika 是 Figma 的一位设计工程与产品经理的复合型人才，她是 FigJam 早期的 PM 之一，现在正主导一款公司将于六月发布的新产品的开发。她被称为 Figma 内部主导从零到一新产品开发的"首选人物"。正如你在我们的对话中会听到的，所有与她共事的人都深深喜爱她。在加入 Figma 之前，Mahika 创办了 Design Nation——一个让本科生更容易获得设计教育的全国性非营利组织，并在 Meta 主导了多个聚焦商务和创作者的产品与发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On this podcast, I bring on a lot of amazing senior product leaders, but there's so much we can learn from stellar on-the-ground product managers like Mahika. In our conversation, we drill into many of the skills that Mahika has cultivated that have contributed to her success, including how to develop a compelling vision, get buy-in for your ideas, how to develop conviction, empathy, the importance of culture, and how to create a culture on your team and within the company, and also how to deal with the constant change that happens within successful organizations.
turns.zh: 在这个播客里，我请来过很多出色的资深产品负责人，但从像 Mahika 这样优秀的"一线"产品经理身上，我们能学到的东西同样很多。在我们的对话中，我们深入探讨了 Mahika 培养出的许多促成她成功的技能，包括如何构建有说服力的愿景、如何为自己的想法争取支持、如何建立信念感与同理心、文化的重要性，以及如何在团队和公司内打造一种文化，还有如何应对成功组织内部持续不断的变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We also spent a bunch of time on how to effectively bring new ideas in your company from zero to one to launch, including getting to a bunch of the stories behind some of Figma's most successful products and features, and how many of them began at hackathons and Maker Weeks. Mahika is a truly special product manager and leader, and I feel fortunate to have had this chance to learn from her. We went quite long on this conversation, but honestly, this could have gone for another two hours. With that, I bring you Mahika Kapoor, after a short word from our sponsors. And if you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it in your favorite podcasting app or YouTube. It's the best way to avoid missing future episodes and it helps the podcast tremendously.
turns.zh: 我们还花了很多时间讨论如何有效地把公司里的新想法从零到一推向发布，包括背后一些 Figma 最成功产品和功能的故事，以及它们中有多少始于黑客马拉松和 Maker Week。Mahika 是一位真正特别的产品经理和领导者，能有机会向她学习，我感到很幸运。我们的对话聊得相当久，但说实话，再聊两个小时也没问题。话不多说，在一段赞助商简介之后，我为你请来 Mahika Kapoor。如果你喜欢这个播客，别忘了在你的播客应用或 YouTube 上订阅并关注。这是避免错过未来节目、并大力支持这个播客最好的方式。

turns.zh: 本期节目由 Lenny's Job Board 赞助。你们当中可能有人知道，也可能不知道，过去几年我一直在经营一项招聘服务。我已经为 30 多家公司推荐了他们的下一位 hires，并为更多公司建立了候选人管道。我有幸与 Ramp、Figma、Shopify 等许多公司，以及一批令人兴奋的年轻初创公司合作，把每家公司与我社区里极具才华的工程师、设计师和产品负责人连接起来。因为它的成功，以及它为企业和求职人创造的价值，我们正在大规模扩展这项服务。我正在测试一种定制化的猎头式服务，并开放了少量名额。我们每个月与一批精选公司合作。如果你需要招募一位关键的产品人才，或快速扩充团队，我很乐意看看能否帮上忙，前往 lennysjobs.com/talent 点击"meet candidates"开始吧，lennysjobs.com/talent。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mahika, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Mahika，非常感谢你来到这里，欢迎来到这个播客。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Thank you for having me, Lenny. I am a huge fan of the podcast and really excited to be chatting today.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。我是这个播客的超级粉丝，今天能聊一聊真的非常激动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to set expectations, this is going to be a Mahika love-fest podcast. And what I want to try to do with our time here is have an archeology of Mahika to understand what you've learned about product and building product, in particular because you are thriving at Figma, which is one of the most interesting and successful tech companies in the world with one of the best product teams in the world. So, basically, I just want to learn as much as I can from what you've learned and what you've done in order to create more Mahikas in the world. That's kind of my goal here because I feel like that would [inaudible 00:05:11].
turns.zh: 先定个调，这会是一期"Mahika 夸夸"播客。我想利用我们这段时间做的，是对 Mahika 来一次"考古"，弄明白你在产品和打造产品这件事上所学到的东西，特别是因为你正在 Figma 如鱼得水——它是全球最有趣、最成功的科技公司之一，拥有全球最顶尖的产品团队之一。所以，说白了，我就是想尽可能多地从你学到的、你做过的事情中汲取经验，好在这个世界上创造更多"Mahika"。这大概就是我的目标，因为我觉得那样会 [inaudible 00:05:11]。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Mildly frightening.
turns.zh: 有点吓人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In a very cool way, not in a creepy way. So, what I did to prep for this conversation is I, as I said, reached out to a bunch of your colleagues at Figma to ask what you're especially strong at. And what I want to do is kind of go through some of these key skills, and they're essentially the core attributes of great product managers and learn from you, learn from what you learned about how doing these things well, and just what you do to be successful at these things. How does that sound?
turns.zh: 是很酷的那种吓人，不是 creepy 的那种。所以，我为这次对话做的准备是，正如我说的，我联系了你在 Figma 的一众同事，问你特别擅长什么。我想做的就是逐一过一遍这些关键技能，它们本质上就是优秀产品经理的核心特质，向你学习，学习你从做这些事中学到的东西，以及你为了把这些事做好到底做了什么。听起来怎么样？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: That sounds good. One thing to call out is that I think when I think about my own PM style, it's definitely not a tick-all-the-boxes style. There are plenty of things that I'm very bad at that PMs are traditionally supposed to be great at, so happy to chat about what makes sense.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。有一点要说明，我觉得当我思考我自己的 PM 风格时，它肯定不是那种"把所有方框都打勾"的风格。有很多事情是我非常不擅长的，而传统上 PM 本应该把这些做到极致，所以我很乐意聊那些有意义的部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's actually really cool. So, let's save that for the end, the things you think you're bad at. The way I see this is a reverse performance review. Here's all the things you're amazing at, let's just go spend all our time on that. But I think that's going to be really important. But just along those lines, what I'm hearing is there's a sense of do the things you are good at really well. This is a trend on the podcast, is lean into your strengths. Is that the way you see it? Do you have thoughts along those lines of just the fact that you've been successful, knowing you have these things you're not amazing at? Then we'll talk.
turns.zh: 好的，那其实很酷。那我们把你自认为不擅长的部分留到结尾。我是这么看的：这是一次反向绩效评估。这里全是你超厉害的地方，我们就把所有时间花在这些上。但我觉得那会非常重要。顺着这个思路，我听到的是一种"把你擅长的事做到极致"的感觉。这也是这个播客里反复出现的主题，就是发挥你的优势。你是这么看的吗？你对"正因为知道自己有些事并不在行却依然成功"这件事有什么想法？那我们接着聊。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: It's important to have two things. One is of course lean into your strengths. I think that PMing is traditionally a sort of generalist role and people fall into it in a number of ways. But most often than not, I hear people fall into it by trying a bunch of other things and then realizing that, "Oh, hey, maybe this PM thing makes more sense for me." So, for me personally, it was I have always been a very left brain, right brain kind of a person. I majored in CS and minored in visual arts. And when I worked as a software engineer, I really missed the design side, and when I worked as a designer, I missed the technical. And moving into product was a really great way to kind of straddle both and have more touch points across the product development cycle. And so, I think that based on how you fell into it, you might have different spikes and different strengths and leaning into those is really important. But for the other things, it's also of course important to have a growth mindset and to constantly be conquering what comes next.
turns.zh: 有两件事很重要。一是当然要发挥你的优势。我觉得 PM 传统上是一个通才型角色，人们以各种方式进入这个岗位。但最常见的是，我听到人们是通过尝试了一堆其他事情之后，才意识到"哦，嘿，也许这个 PM 的活儿更适合我"。就我个人而言，我一直是个左右脑兼具的人。我主修计算机科学，辅修视觉艺术。当我做软件工程师的时候，我真的很怀念设计的一面；而当我做设计师的时候，我又怀念技术的一面。转做产品是一个非常好的方式，让我能横跨两边，在产品开发周期中有更多的触点。所以，我觉得基于你是怎么进入这个角色的，你可能会有不同的"尖峰"和不同的优势，发挥这些非常重要。但对其他那些事，当然同样重要的是要有一个成长型心态，不断地去攻克接下来出现的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Okay, so I'll save the stuff you think you're bad at for later. Let's start with the stuff you're basic at. Okay. So, the first is vision. So, Sho Kuwamoto, VP of product at Figma told me that, "Mahika is really great at creating a vision and getting people to see what she sees. She's working on a new project now and put together one of the best pitches I've ever seen internally at what it could become, why it'd be differentiated, et cetera. And like every new project, this had up and downs, but she's incredibly driven to keep the flame alive throughout these ups and downs." Can you just talk about what you've learned about doing this well, creating a compelling vision, getting people excited, getting buy-in for big ideas?
turns.zh: 好的，酷。那我先把你认为自己不擅长的部分留到后面。我们先从你 basics 好的地方开始。好。第一个是愿景（vision）。Figma 的产品副总裁 Sho Kuwamoto 告诉我："Mahika 非常擅长构建愿景，并让人们看到她所看到的东西。她现在正在做一个新项目，并拿出了我在公司内部见过最棒的 pitch 之一，讲清楚了它能成为什么、为什么会有差异化，等等。和每个新项目一样，这其中有起有伏，但她有着不可思议的驱动力，在这些起伏中始终让这团火保持燃烧。" 你能聊聊你从把这件事做好中学到了什么吗——构建有说服力的愿景、让人们兴奋、为大的想法争取支持？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So, my take is that vision is everything. It is really important to create a vision that you believe in, that your team believes in and that your company believes in. Because the reality of the product development cycle is that it's so messy, it's so chaotic. You're going to have extreme highs and extreme lows. You're going to march in a certain direction only to hear from your users that it might just be the wrong direction, and totally pivot. And in order to ensure that moments that are not discouraging, but rather, learning opportunities for your team team, it's so important to be anchored on that singular vision because then any step along the way feels like forward progress.
turns.zh: 当然可以。我的看法是，愿景就是一切。构建一个你相信、你的团队相信、你的公司也相信的愿景，真的非常重要。因为产品开发周期的现实是，它是如此混乱、如此混沌。你会经历极度的巅峰和极度的低谷。你会朝着某个方向前进，结果却从用户那里听说那可能完全是错的方向，然后彻底转向。为了让这些时刻不让人气馁，而是成为团队的学习机会，锚定在那个唯一的愿景上就极其重要，因为这样一来，沿途的每一步都像是向前迈进了。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So, first, just want to underscore the importance of having that vision and that perspective on if you and your team do your job correctly what does the world look like? In terms of crafting a compelling vision, I think that there's sort of a few aspects. The first is that you cannot go into a vacuum and come out with a compelling vision that does not exist. You have to be fundamentally inseparable from your users, and also, fundamentally inseparable from your team. And so, I think that there is sort of this important cross-pollination of functions that is really important in crafting a compelling vision. You want to always ensure that there are research insights that help you feel what a user is feeling. You want to ensure that there are beautiful designs and prototypes that help communicate what this future world looks like, and you also want to root it in engineering and feasibility. And you want to be constantly, even in the vision phase, assuring that what you're marching after is something that is achievable and something that you can work towards.
turns.zh: 所以，首先，我想强调拥有那个愿景的重要性，以及那种"如果你和你的团队把工作做到位，世界会是什么样子"的视角。在构思一个有说服力的愿景方面，我觉得有几个方面。第一，你不可能走进一个真空、然后带着一个根本不存在的有说服力的愿景走出来。你必须与你的用户密不可分，也必须与你的团队密不可分。所以，我觉得在构建有说服力的愿景时，这种职能之间的"交叉授粉"非常重要。你希望始终确保有研究洞察，能帮你感受用户的感受。你希望确保有精美的设计和原型，能帮助传达那个未来世界的样子，你也希望把它扎根于工程和可行性。即使在愿景阶段，你也要不断确认你追逐的东西是可实现的、是你可以努力达成的。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, I think a lot of folks when they think about visioning, they kind of think about, "Okay, how do we start from scratch and learn about the user and then translate that into designs and then translate that into engineering?" And it becomes this very almost linear process. And I think that to the extent that you can have this cross-pollination of ideas and people working together, that leads to a really strong vision. And there's this book that I love called The Medici Effect, which basically talks about how when people come from different places and you have that confluence of ideas, that leads to innovation at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 所以，我觉得很多人在想到"愿景"时，会想"好，我们怎么从零开始、了解用户，然后把它转化成设计，再转化成工程？" 于是这就变成了一个几乎线性的过程。而我认为，在你能让这种想法的交叉授粉、让人们一起协作的程度上，才会产生真正扎实的愿景。有一本我很喜欢的书叫《The Medici Effect》（美第奇效应），它基本上讲的是当来自不同地方的人汇聚、思想交汇时，最终会带来创新。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: The second piece is, okay, once you have your vision, once you have talked to your users and built up your perspective and things like that, it's like how do you communicate it internally and how do you help everyone around you see what you're seeing? And I think something that's really unique about Figma is that it is a fundamentally very, very detail-oriented culture. And it's also a company that very much practices what it preaches in terms of the future being visual communication. And so, I've found that words will only get you so far. So, when I put together a vision with my team at Figma, it's all about not just your traditional, "Okay, here are pain points. And then, here are solutions. And then, here is the timeline and costing." But rather how can you bring all of those things together and how can a vision pitch effectively be pain point, solution, proof point, pain point solution proof point?
turns.zh: 第二点是，好，一旦你有了愿景，一旦你和用户聊过、建立起了你的视角等等，问题就变成了：你如何在内部沟通它，如何让周围的人都看到你所看到的？我觉得 Figma 有一点非常独特，那就是它是一个从根本上非常、非常注重细节的文化。它也是一家真正践行"未来是视觉化沟通"理念的公司。所以，我发现光靠文字只能带你走这么远。因此，当我和 Figma 的团队一起构建愿景时，关键不只是你传统的"好，这里是痛点。然后，这里是解决方案。然后，这里是时间表和成本。" 而是你怎么把所有这些东西汇聚在一起，一份愿景 pitch 怎么才能有效地呈现为：痛点、解决方案、证明点，痛点、解决方案、证明点？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Because at the end of the day, simply describing a product idea in words is not as compelling as seeing a testimonial from a user on top of a prototype or a mock, and really feeling the pain points.
turns.zh: 因为归根结底，仅仅用文字描述一个产品想法，远没有在一份原型或模型之上看到一条用户感言、真切地感受到那些痛点来得有说服力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example that we could talk about? I know you can't talk about the product you're working on yet, but from the past of a vision that you crafted maybe to share what the vision was or how you came to that to make this even more real?
turns.zh: 有没有我们可以具体聊的例子？我知道你还不能谈你正在做的产品，但能不能从过去聊一个你构建的愿景，分享一下那个愿景是什么、或者你是怎么得出它的，让这一切更真实？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So, before I was working on the new product, I was working on the FigJam team, and I was an early member of the FigJam team. And whiteboarding was something that really took off during the pandemic because it was the first time that people were not together in office, couldn't jam together, couldn't just throw up a whiteboard behind them physically. And so, there was kind of this question of, okay, how do you combat these disparate teammates and pull them together into a common space? And I think that when we think about FigJam and what success might look like for FigJam, a part of it that I was really invested in was the meetings experience. And specifically, what the world would look like if we were successful at bringing people together into a common space?
turns.zh: 在我做新产品之前，我在 FigJam 团队，是 FigJam 团队的早期成员。白板在疫情期间真正火了起来，因为那是人们第一次不在一起办公，没法一起 jam、没法在身后随手立起一块实体白板。所以，就出现了这样一个问题：好，你怎么把这些分散的队友聚合起来，拉进一个共同的空间？我觉得，当我们思考 FigJam 以及 FigJam 的成功可能是什么样子时，我特别投入其中一部分，那就是会议体验。具体来说，如果我们成功地把人们汇聚到一个共同空间，世界会是什么样子？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And one of the early insights was, okay, what is the most common meeting that takes place in a FigJam file? It's a brainstorm, right? It's like you have a bunch of people, you've coming together and they're dropping a bunch of stickies and stuff like that. And so, you have this proof point of an activity that works really well inside of a FigJam file. But then, at the same time, something that's really interesting about FigJam, people often ask, "Oh, you guys are Figma. How do you guys use Figma as a company?" And it's kind of interesting because I feel like we use Figma the way that everyone uses Figma, but we use FigJam on steroids. Every single activity in this company is done in FigJam. Our product reviews are in there, our Gantt charts are in there, our bug bashes are in there. Every single thing is in FigJam.
turns.zh: 早期的一个洞察是：在一个 FigJam 文件里，最常见的会议是什么？是头脑风暴，对吧？就是一群人聚在一起，丢一堆便利贴之类的东西。所以，你在 FigJam 文件里有一个"运作得非常好"的活动作为证明点。但与此同时，FigJam 有一个很有意思的地方，人们常问："哦，你们是 Figma。你们公司自己怎么用 Figma？" 这挺有意思的，因为我觉得我们像所有人用 Figma 那样用 Figma，但我们用 FigJam 是"加了buff"的。这家公司的每一项活动都在 FigJam 里进行。我们的产品评审在里面，我们的甘特图在里面，我们的 bug bash 在里面。每一件事都在 FigJam 里。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And there was this gap between the way that we were using FigJam as a company and the way that the rest of the world was using it, but brainstorms were working. And so, you kind of think, "Okay, what's unique about a brainstorm?" And you talk to your users and you're like, "Why does a brainstorm make so much more sense in a FigJam file than anything else?" And what it comes down to is brainstorms are this incredibly democratizing process. It's this process where ideas can come from anywhere, where it's not the loudest or the most important person in the room who's doing the talking, but it's everyone altogether. And you're able to elicit reactions from people who are more quiet in a meeting or people who may prefer to ideate on their own before coming out to everyone and things like that.
turns.zh: 于是，我们作为一家公司使用 FigJam 的方式，和世界其他地方使用它的方式之间，出现了一道鸿沟，但头脑风暴是行得通的。所以你会想："好，头脑风暴有什么特别之处？" 你去和用户聊，你会想："为什么头脑风暴在 FigJam 文件里比在别的地方都更合理？" 归结起来就是：头脑风暴是一个极其民主化的过程。在这个过程中，想法可以来自任何地方，不是房间里嗓门最大或最重要的人在说话，而是所有人一起。你能够引出那些在会议上更安静的人，或者那些更愿意先自己想清楚再面向大家的人等等的反应。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, we started with the seed of brainstorms being this highly democratic process. And what you see is that in most other scenarios, meetings are very one way. You have one person talking, and everyone else reacting. This is true of a team kickoff. This is true of an all-hands. This is true of basically every sort of scenario. And so, what we fundamentally started marching towards was how can we create this world where the generative nature of a brainstorm is basically the norm in other kinds of meetings. Where a team kickoff is not just a PM and a designer handing mocks to an engineer, but it's everyone leaving stickies and everyone commenting at the same time, or everyone leaving...
turns.zh: 所以，我们从"头脑风暴是一种高度民主的过程"这个种子出发。而你会看到，在大多数其他场景里，会议是非常单向的。一个人讲，其他人反应。团队 kickoff 是这样，全员大会是这样，基本上每一种场景都是这样。所以，我们从根本上开始朝着这样一个方向前进：我们如何创造这样一个世界——头脑风暴那种"生成式"的特质，成为其他类型会议的常态。比如团队 kickoff 不只是 PM 和设计师把模型交给工程师，而是所有人同时贴便利贴、同时评论，或者所有人一起……

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: We have this ritual called Kudos Boards inside of FigJam, where everyone will shower each other with love and just kind call out their teammates for what they've done over the last week or so. And so how can we ensure that those kind of rituals are in our templates and that we're teaching people how to take any meeting and make it more democratic? And then, you anchor on this vision around, okay, what does a more democratic workplace look like and how can we get people to anchor around that and how can we get people to get into the flow? So, then we started launching features like music, like voting, that really help you get into flow when you're in that pile together.
turns.zh: 我们在 FigJam 里有一个叫 Kudos Boards 的仪式，大家会互相表达爱意，就只是点名表扬队友过去一周左右所做的事。所以，我们怎么才能确保这类仪式进入我们的模板、怎么教人们把任何一场会议都变得更民主？然后，你锚定在这个愿景上：好，一个更民主的职场是什么样子，我们怎么让人们锚定在它上面，我们怎么让人们进入那个"心流"？于是我们开始发布像音乐、像投票这样的功能，真的能帮你在大家挤在一起时进入心流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a cool example. I'm trying to be this archeologist studying what you're describing and breaking it apart. So, what I'm hearing essentially is there's this insight that you find of, "Oh, here's a way we should think about the way future of work. It should be more democratic," building on this idea of brainstorming, which is one of the most inspiring ways of working where it's not just someone sitting in a silo. And then, you take that and create kind of a, "Here's what the world could look like if we could make everything this feel this way, very democratic." And then there's this pitch that you eventually make of, "Here's the product." And you talked about how the way you pitch it is, "Here's a pain, here's a solution, and here's a proof point of that solution," could be a testimonial or some data, I imagine.
turns.zh: 这是一个超酷的例子。我试着像那个考古学家一样，研究你描述的、并把它拆开。所以，我听到的本质上是：你找到了这样一个洞察——"哦，这是一种我们应该用来思考未来工作的方式。它应该更民主"——它建立在"头脑风暴"这个概念之上，而头脑风暴是最鼓舞人心的工作方式之一，不是某个人坐在孤岛里。然后，你拿它创造了一个"如果能让一切都这种感觉、都这么民主，世界会是什么样子"。然后，你最终做出了这样一个 pitch："这就是那个产品。" 你谈到你做 pitch 的方式是"这里是痛点，这里是解决方案，这里是这个解决方案的证明点"——我猜可能是一条感言或某些数据。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Definitely. I think that when you're actually presenting a vision, one of the most important things is that there is a single artifact that the team is creating together. So, I think a common occurrence is to have the research readout, followed by the design crit, followed by the product review. And that's fine, that works in a lot of instances, but then you have every team member thinking that their own deliverable is what they need to pour all their energy into. And what you actually want is for everyone to feel incredible ownership and incredible passion about this combined deliverable, so that it's a unified team who believes a singular set of insights.
turns.zh: 当然。我觉得，当你真正在呈现一个愿景时，最重要的事情之一，是团队在一起创造的是一个单一的作品（artifact）。所以，常见的做法是：先有研究汇报，接着是设计 crit，然后是产品评审。这没问题，在很多情况下都行得通，但那样每个团队成员都会觉得自己的交付物才是自己需要倾注全部精力的东西。而你真正想要的是，让每个人对这个组合起来的交付物都拥有极强的归属感和热情，这样它就是一个信念统一的团队，相信同一组洞察。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what's an example of that? Is it like a deck in Figma?
turns.zh: 那能举个例子吗？是像 Figma 里的一个 deck 吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So, we often make our decks in Figma, and I think that we lean heavily into designing and prototyping even before a project gets a green light. So, I think that's something that's really unique about Figma is normally you will talk about the market space or the opportunity of the sizing, and then decide to invest. Versus Figma is very much a see to believe and see to feel that emotional pull towards this is something worth investing in.
turns.zh: 对，正是。我们经常在 Figma 里做 deck，我觉得我们会在项目甚至还没获得绿灯之前，就大量投入设计和原型制作。所以，我觉得这是 Figma 很独特的一点：通常你会先谈市场规模或机会的大小，然后才决定投资。而 Figma 则非常强调"先看见、才相信"，先看见、才感受到那种"这值得投资"的情感牵引。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, that's what I was trying to get to is how do you actually deliver a vision? So, a lot of people, " Here, I need to create a vision. I'm going to write out a paragraph or a memo describing it." You can create mock-ups. The way you're describing it, essentially, is make it as real as possible, not just mocks, but actual prototypes potentially. Many people don't have design skills or designers on their team or engineering skills to build a prototype. Is there anything you can share for how to do this where you don't have those skills?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以，这就是我想问的：你到底怎么交付一个愿景？很多人是"好，我需要创造一个愿景。我要写一段话或一份备忘录来描述它。" 你可以做 mock-up。你描述的方式，本质上是：让它尽可能真实，不只是 mock，还可能是真正的原型。很多人没有设计技能，团队里也没有设计师或工程能力去建原型。你能在"没有这些技能"的情况下分享一些做法吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah. Well, the good thing is that with AI, it's getting way easier. So-
turns.zh: 可以。好的一点是，有了 AI，这件事越来越容易了。所以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: True.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: A couple of weeks ago, Cognition launched, which for those who don't know, is a startup that made this AI agent called Devin, which can code anything for you, supposedly. It definitely took Twitter by storm and got me super stoked. And so, I think something that's interesting about the current AI revolution is that it's very much lowering the floor to starting out and to building something. And so, recently, I was doing a chat with David Huang from Replit, and he's the head of marketing and design at Replit. And he was basically talking about how if Replit does their job right, you start seeing it as your technical co-founder. And I think, conversely at Figma we kind of think about if we're doing our job, maybe in the future people will think about Figma as their designer co-founder, where you can go in and use it to start bringing things into existence.
turns.zh: 几周前，Cognition 发布了——不了解的人，它是一家初创公司，做出了一个叫 Devin 的 AI agent，据说能为你写任何代码。它确实在 Twitter 上掀起了风暴，让我超级兴奋。所以，我觉得当前这场 AI 革命有意思的地方在于，它正在大幅降低"起步、去构建某样东西"的门槛。最近，我和 Replit 的 David Huang 聊了聊，他是 Replit 的营销和设计负责人。他 basically 在讲，如果 Replit 把工作做到位，你会开始把它看作你的技术联合创始人。而我觉得，反过来说，在 Figma 我们 kind of 认为，如果我们把工作做到位，也许未来人们会把 Figma 看作他们的设计联合创始人，你可以进去用它开始把东西变成现实。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So, I think one is, yeah, I do think that we're just trending in a direction, and this was not true a year ago, where the floor to building something is just so much lower. So, that's one piece. I think the second piece is just go around and ask people. And so, for example, for the project that I'm currently working on, I used a hackathon to pitch it. And basically, I built conviction in the idea many months before the hackathon, and I was verbally pitching it. And it was kind of like, "Oh yeah, maybe at some point in the future we would make an investment like this."
turns.zh: 所以，第一点是，是的，我确实觉得我们正朝着一个方向走，而且这一点一年前还不存在，那就是构建某样东西的门槛真的低太多了。这是其一。我觉得第二点是：直接去周围找人问。比如，对我现在做的这个项目，我用一个黑客马拉松来 pitch 它。basically，我在黑客马拉松之前好几个月就对这个想法建立了信念，并一直在口头 pitch 它。当时有点像"哦对，也许未来某个时候我们会做这样的投资。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: But what actually ended up happening was we have this concept called Maker Week, which is our internal hackathon, where the entire company goes on pause for a week. And I think that most people think that, "Oh, hackathons are only a time for engineers to build." And I think that that's one of the biggest mistakes ever. I think that anyone can have an idea and can... Literally, what I did was walk around the New York office asking every single person, "Will you work on this thing with me?" And eventually, someone says yes, and then you can use that to build momentum, grow the team, and build something great. But I think that never letting your own skills stop you from going out there making a pitch and then turning that into reality is really important.
turns.zh: 但真正发生的是，我们有一个叫 Maker Week 的概念，这是我们内部的黑客马拉松，整个公司会停摆一周。我觉得大多数人以为"哦，黑客马拉松只是工程师用来构建的时间。" 而我认为那是有史以来最大的错误之一。我觉得任何人都可以有想法，并且可以…… 说真的，我当时做的就是在新 York 办公室里转，问每一个我遇到的人："你愿意和我一起做这件事吗？" 最终，有人说是，然后你就能用它来建立势头、壮大团队、做出很棒的东西。但我觉得，永远不要让自己的技能成为阻止你走出去做 pitch、然后把那变成现实的理由，这一点非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love both of these points and pieces of advice. I feel like I always say that if a PM has a designer partner that can just help them with a deck or help them with ideas, that you're such a superpower, everything just looks so much more interesting when you have a designer helping you craft your idea. And the way you describe it is pretty simple. Just go ask people for help because you're probably going to find someone that's going to help you out.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这两点建议。我总觉得，如果一个 PM 有个设计师搭档能帮他们做 deck 或出主意，那你就像开了挂一样，有人帮你想法做包装时，一切都看起来有意思得多。而你描述的方式相当简单：直接去问别人要帮助，因为你很可能找到愿意帮你的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned conviction, so that's a great segue to else where I wanted to go next. So, I asked Yuhki, chief product officer at Figma, about your strengths. And he told me that you get extremely strong conviction extremely quickly. He said that this strong conviction allows you to navigate the messy journey from zero to one and rally your team in a really powerful way. He actually wanted me to ask you this very question, how do you get to this strong conviction? And how much of it is to true deep conviction, versus there's an inkling of instinct that this is going to work and then you profit on the sense of conviction to get people rallying behind you and to kind of take this leap of faith?
turns.zh: 你提到了 conviction（信念感），那是很好的过渡，正好引向我接下来想去的方向。我向 Figma 的首席产品官 Yuhki 问了你的优势。他告诉我，你能极快地建立起极强的信念感。他说，这种强烈的信念感让你能够驾驭从零到一的混乱旅程，并以一种非常有力量的方式把团队团结起来。他其实想让我亲自问你这个问题：你是怎么建立起这种强烈信念感的？又有多少是真正 deep 的信念，多少是"有一种这能成事的直觉苗头"，然后你靠这种信念感让人们团结在你身后、让人愿意迈出那一步？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think that one of the most important things for a PM to create for their team is momentum. You have to constantly be creating forward progress, probably towards that vision that we were just talking about. But I'm a huge proponent of Jeff Bezos's one-way doors, two-way doors framework. And I think that especially in a software company, most things are two-way doors. You can come back. And so, it's so important to have an opinion and use that opinion to anchor people around and have people react to. So, I used to work at Meta before I worked at Figma, and Meta basically distilled the product role into two core capabilities. One was product sense and one was execution. And when you think about product sense, it's like, okay, what is product sense? It's like a really abstract term. And at the end of the day, I think product sense is just having good intuition.
turns.zh: 我觉得，PM 能为团队创造的最重要的事情之一，就是 momentum（势头）。你必须不断地创造向前推进的进展，大概率是朝着我们刚才谈的那个愿景。但我非常推崇 Jeff Bezos 的"单向门、双向门"框架。我觉得尤其在软件公司，大多数事情都是双向门。你可以回来。所以，有观点、并用这个观点把人们锚定住、让人们去反应，这非常重要。我在来 Figma 之前曾在 Meta 工作，Meta 基本上把产品角色提炼为两个核心能力。一个是 product sense（产品感），一个是 execution（执行力）。当你思考 product sense 时，会觉得：好，什么是 product sense？这是个很抽象的术语。而归根结底，我觉得 product sense 就是拥有好的直觉。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, there's this question about, okay, how do you build up intuition? And I think that it's just by having this insatiable curiosity and talking to users at every chance you get. So, I would go to dinners and grill the people around me on how they use Figma and how they use FigJam. And I think when you have a conversation with someone, it's so much more powerful in terms of getting those anecdotes to stick in your head. And what actually happens is once you start having enough conversations, let's say you start with conversations ABC, then you progress to conversations DEF, over time you build this almost repository or library of conversations that you can draw from as you're making product decisions. And so, I think that that's a really powerful thing to lean into as you're thinking about, "Okay, which path do we go down?"
turns.zh: 于是就有这个问题：好，你如何建立起直觉？我觉得就是靠那种永不满足的好奇心，以及抓住一切机会和用户交谈。所以，我会去吃晚饭，并盘问周围的人他们怎么用 Figma、怎么用 FigJam。我觉得当你和一个人对话时，那些轶事会牢牢地印在你脑子里，这比别的方式有力得多。真正发生的是，一旦你开始有足够的对话，假设从 A、B、C 几段对话开始，然后推进到 D、E、F，随着时间推移，你就建立起了一个几乎像仓库或图书馆一样的对话库，可以从中汲取，来做产品决策。所以我觉得，在你思考"好，我们走哪条路"时，这是一个非常值得依靠的东西。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Now, there's the question of in the absence of any external signal, what can you do? And I think that a very common thing, especially for PMs who are younger in their career, is to think that your opinion isn't right or might not be reflective of what the user thinks. So, you think, "Okay, I believe this," and at the end of the day, everyone has an opinion, right? So, "I think this, but what do I know compared to these people who've been in my company for 10 years?" Or, "What do I know compared to my users who are using the product?" And so, then I think what might happen in those instances is you kind of start from nothing, you start from zero and you're like, "Okay, I'm going to build up from zero and gather all of these insights to get to a good place."
turns.zh: 那么，在没有外部信号的情况下，你能做什么？我觉得一个很常见的现象，尤其是对于那些职业生涯还比较早期的 PM，就是会认为自己想法不对、或者可能并不能反映用户的想法。所以你会想："好，我相信这个"，但归根结底，每个人都有自己的观点，对吧？所以"我觉得这个，但比起在公司待了 10 年的人，我能知道什么？" 或者"比起正在用这个产品的用户，我能知道什么？" 于是我觉得，在这些情况下可能发生的是，你从一无所有开始，从零开始，然后想"好，我要从零搭建，收集所有这些洞察，才能达到一个好的状态。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And I think my take is that putting out an idea, even if it's totally wrong, is a much better catalyst for getting to a good solution because people are much more likely to react to an idea than to nothing. So, if it's the right idea, then they'll be like, "Oh my God, yes, let's totally do that." And if it's wrong, then it's like, okay, then they will take you in a different direction and you end up with something that's probably much more opinionated than if you hadn't put anything out there. And so, it was funny, one piece of advice that I got from Yuhki when I was working on my vision sprint was like, "Okay, when you go into research, you want to go in with something that's at least an A- idea, or you think is at least an A- idea. Because if you talk to users and you learn something about it, that's awesome. Get to an A+. If not, at least you're not at a B." And so, I think that having-
turns.zh: 而我的看法是，抛出一个想法，哪怕它完全错了，也是通向好解决方案更好的催化剂，因为人们更容易对一个想法做出反应，而不是对"什么都没有"做出反应。所以，如果它是对的，他们会说"哦我的天，对，就这么做。" 如果是错的，那他们会把你带向另一个方向，你最终得到的东西，可能比如果你什么都不抛出时要"更有观点"得多。所以当时有个好玩的事，Yuhki 在我做愿景冲刺时给我的建议是："好，当你去做研究时，你要带着一个至少是 A- 的想法进去，或者你觉得至少是 A- 的想法。因为如果你和用户聊、从中学到东西，那太棒了，做到 A+。如果没有，至少你不是 B。" 所以我觉得，拥有——

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: If not, at least you're not at a B. And so I think that having that early conviction, being willing to communicate it, being willing to get feedback from other folks in your team, have them react to it, then get users to react to it, is so important, but then also something that's equally important when you have "high conviction", quote, unquote, is to be willing to kill your darlings if you hear something that tells you otherwise. You need to be so sort of strong opinions weekly held. And if you get external signal that's telling you something different, you should be ready to pivot and have that agility to do so.
turns.zh: 如果没有，至少你不是 B。所以我觉得，拥有那种 early conviction、愿意去沟通它、愿意从团队其他人那里获得反馈、让他们对它做出反应，然后让用户也对它做出反应，这非常重要；但同样重要的是，当你有那种所谓"高信念感"时，如果你听到相反的信号，也要愿意"kill your darlings"（放弃你心爱的东西）。你需要那种"观点很强、但随时可被推翻"的态度。如果你得到告诉你不一样的外部信号，你要准备好转向，并拥有那样敏捷的能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of PMs that kind of worry about having too strong of an opinion and being like, "Here's what we're doing," because then there's this like, "Oh, okay, they just want us to do the thing they want us to do, and we don't have a voice. We don't have a chance to influence." It seems like you find a really magical balance of strong opinion of like, "Here's what we should be doing," but people still love working with you and don't feel like... I haven't heard like, "Oh, she just tells us what to bill." What advice do you have there of just finding that balance and making it clear? It's just my idea. We can change it.
turns.zh: 有很多 PM 会担心拥有太强的观点，比如"这就是我们要做的"，因为那样就会有"哦好，他们只是想让我们做他们想做的事，我们没声音。我们没机会去影响。" 看起来你找到了一种神奇的 balancing——既有"这是我们应该做的"这种强观点，但人们依然喜欢和你共事，不觉得……我没听过"哦，她就是告诉我们该 build 什么。" 你在这方面有什么建议，就是找到那种平衡、并说清楚"这只是我的想法。我们可以改。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I would say that speaking about weaknesses, having such strong conviction absolutely has downsides. In particular, it's possible that it doesn't have the desired effect. So for example, my designer who I work with, his name is Kean, he's so talented. We work like this. Literally for most of last year, we had an hour long one- on-one every single day and still that wasn't enough-
turns.zh: 我要说，讲到弱点，拥有这么强的信念感绝对有 downsides。特别是，它可能达不到想要的效果。比如，和我一起工作的设计师，他叫 Kean，特别有才华。我们这样工作。literally 去年大部分时间，我们每天都有一小时的 one-on-one，但那还不够——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyday?
turns.zh: 每天？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: ... meeting time. Yes. We basically work together like this, but he also told me that when I joined the company, he was like, "Who is this girl and why does she have so many opinions?" And so I think that something that I have learned to do over time, and I think that's something that's a good sort of thing to lean into if you are a PM who has strong opinions, is to be very direct about how much you care about your opinions. So now, I'll do this thing where I'll be like, "Oh, I think we should do this, but I feel like medium confidence on it." So if you feel stronger like, "I defer to you," and always being very, very, very explicit about like, "I feel really strongly about this," or, "This is my hypothesis," or, "I do not have an opinion here. I defer to you."
turns.zh: ……会议时间。对。我们 basically 这样一起工作，但他也告诉我，当我刚加入公司时，他是那种"这姑娘是谁，为什么有这么多观点？" 所以我觉得，随着时间推移我学会做的一件事——而且我觉得如果你是一个有强观点的 PM，这是很值得依靠的一点——就是非常直接地说明你有多在意你的观点。所以现在，我会做这样的事，我会说"哦，我觉得我们应该这样做，但我对它的信心是中等。" 所以如果你感觉更强烈，就"我听你的"，并且永远都要非常、非常、非常明确地表示"我对这个真的有很强的感觉"，或者"这是我的假设"，或者"我在这里没有观点。我听你的。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think the second thing that I would mention that is really important in order to do this correctly is... So I have a very direct communication style. I will never sugarcoat anything. I'll never say I like something if I don't like something. If I'm in a meeting and someone tells me they don't agree with me, I will tell them I don't agree with them back. In return, I really like it when people are very direct with me. And so I think that whenever I join a team or whenever I start working with a new person, I always let them know. I'm always like, :I am very direct and if you disagree with me, I want to know that."
turns.zh: 我觉得，为了正确地做这件事，我要提到的第二件非常重要的事是…… 我有非常直接的沟通风格。我从不粉饰任何东西。我不喜欢的东西，我绝不会说我喜欢。如果我在会议上，有人告诉我他们不认同我，我会直接告诉他们我也不认同他们。作为回报，我也很喜欢别人对我非常直接。所以我觉得，每当我加入一个团队、或者开始和一个新人合作，我都会让他们知道。我总是说："我非常直接，如果你不认同我，我希望知道这一点。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Because I think sometimes what can happen is really strongly minded PMs can go into a conversation and can be like, "Oh, I think we should do X," even though they actually feel medium confidence about X. And then the rest of the room is like, "Oh, my God. That PM feels so strongly about doing X that I'm not going to say anything because they clearly have so much conviction in X." And what you actually want is for everyone to feel comfortable speaking up. And so creating that culture where everyone feels comfortable giving their opinion and communicating their level of confidence is really important.
turns.zh: 因为我觉得有时候会发生的是，信念感很强的 PM 会走进一场对话，然后说"哦，我觉得我们应该做 X"，哪怕他们其实对 X 只有中等信心。然后房间里其他人就会像"哦我的天。那个 PM 对做 X 有这么强的感觉，那我就不说了，因为她显然对 X 有那么强的信念。" 而你真正想要的是，让每个人都觉得舒服、敢于发声。所以，打造一种让每个人都舒服地给出自己观点、并沟通自己信心水平的文化，真的非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So this direct communication point you made, somebody shared this quote, Alice Ching, who I think your EM said this about you that she's in awe of how direct you are, especially how you can make it not personal and help people focus on the matter at hand. Any other advice you have there for people to, one, either be more direct and successful in that being directness? Or is there an example you can share where, because I think people hear this, they're like, "Oh yeah, I'm going to be direct. I'm going to be so direct, it's going to be great," and then it's so hard to actually do, so is there maybe an example that comes to mind of here's something you did recently of like, "Oh, wow. Okay, I see what she's talking about"?
turns.zh: 你提到的这种直接沟通，有人分享了一句引语，Alice Ching——我想是你的 EM——这样评价你：她对你那种直接感到惊叹，尤其是你能做到不针对个人、帮人们聚焦在眼前的事情上。你还有什么建议，关于人们怎么（一）变得更直接、并在这种直接中取得成功？或者有没有一个你最近做过的例子，比如"哦，哇，好，我明白她说的意思了"？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So I think that directness only works if it's two-way. If it is one person being really direct with another person and then the other person being afraid to talk, you will end up in probably a not great relationship where communication is only going one way and both people will be in their own head. The person being direct will be like, "Why is the other person not responding to my feedback?" And then the other person will be like, "Why am I the only one getting so much feedback?" Meta, where I used to work, had this phrase, "Feedback as a gift," and I so deeply believe in this. And in order to really lean into that phrase and really embody it, I think it's really important that feedback is this constantly flowing thing, not something that happens once or twice a year when you have an official feedback cycle.
turns.zh: 我觉得直接只有双向才有效。如果是一个人非常直接地对另一个人，而另一个人却不敢开口，你最终会处在一个可能不太好的关系里，沟通只朝一个方向流动，两个人都会活在自己的脑袋里。那个直接的人会想："为什么另一个人对我的反馈没反应？" 而另一个人会想："为什么只有我一个人收到这么多反馈？" 我以前工作的 Meta 有句话叫"Feedback as a gift"（反馈是礼物），我深深认同这句话。要真正践行这句话、真正体现它，我觉得非常重要的一点是，反馈应该是持续流动的东西，而不是一年只有一两次、在正式反馈周期里才发生的事。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And the way that I try and create this culture of constant direct communication, constant feedback is if you have feedback to give someone else, I think you can start by asking, "Hey, do you have feedback from me?" And kind of taking the feedback first so then that person feels like, "Okay, maybe I have my way of seeing this situation. Let me communicate that and get off my chest." And then when you give your feedback, it's sort of even. And then feedback in my opinion is something that you should always act on. So then to the extent that you can as soon as possible put that into effect and be like, "Okay, I'm hearing this. I'm going to do XYZ in order to combat that." I think then that incentivizes the other person to do the same.
turns.zh: 我尝试打造这种"持续直接沟通、持续反馈"文化的方式是：如果你要给别人反馈，我觉得你可以先问"嘿，你对我有什么反馈吗？" 先把反馈接过来，这样那个人就会觉得"好，也许我也有我看这件事的角度。让我把它说出来、一吐为快。" 然后当你给反馈时，就平衡了。而且在我看来，反馈是你永远应该付诸行动的东西。所以，在你能做到的范围内，尽快把它落实，像"好，我听到了这个。我要做 XYZ 来应对它。" 我觉得这样会激励对方也这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let me quickly summarize what we've gone through so far in our archaeological study, and then I'm going to drill into a specific trait. So one is just having a really powerful vision that people get really excited about. And the way you described it is kind of find an insight about how you think people could be, in this example, how people could be working maybe through this brainstorm approach and then kind of expanding that into something where this is what would happen if we achieve this in the future, and this is what the world could look like, and that's something people get really excited about.
turns.zh: 好，让我快速总结一下我们到目前为止在这项"考古研究"里过的内容，然后我要深入一个具体的特质。一是，拥有一个真正有力、让人们非常兴奋的愿景。你描述的方式有点像：找到一个关于"你认为人们可以怎样"的洞察——在这个例子中，是人们可以怎样通过这种头脑风暴的方式工作——然后把它扩展成"如果我们未来实现了这个，会发生什么"，以及"世界会是什么样子"，而那是人们会非常兴奋的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So kind of creating compelling vision, being able to communicate it with, and in your experience, communicating with prototypes and mocks is the way that you find it to be most effective. Also, just getting to strong conviction, whether it's real or not, but it sounds like it's actually very genuine about an idea and making it clear. You're very excited about this and here's how it's going to be amazing for the business and the company, and here's why you should be excited about it. Also, you talked about being very direct and being very honest and basically radical candor as some people describe it. First of all, is there anything else I missed specifically before I drill into one of these?
turns.zh: 也就是，构建有说服力的愿景，并能沟通它——在你的经验里，用原型和 mock 来沟通是你觉得最有效的方式。还有，建立强烈的信念感，不管它是真还是假，但听起来你对一个想法是真正发自内心的，并把它说清楚。你非常兴奋，并讲清楚它对业务和公司会有多棒、你为什么应该为它兴奋。你也谈到了非常直接、非常诚实，基本上就是有些人说的"radical candor"（极度坦诚）。首先，在我深入其中一个之前，还有什么我漏掉的吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: That sounds right.
turns.zh: 听起来没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So kind of along these lines, something else that came up a bunch of in my emails with folks that you work with is how you build hype really effectively, and you talked about this a bit of just creating momentum about an idea. So you got this idea, get everyone pitch it, get everyone excited, and then it just continues to build hype and momentum. So a quote from Karl Jiang, who is on your team maybe, he said, "I feel no PM has ever got me so hyped about a feature." And Yuhki said that you overcome people's doubts by building hype and hacking hype is the way described it. Talk about this and why do you think it's important and how you actually go about doing this.
turns.zh: 好的，酷。顺着这个思路，在我和共事的人邮件往来中反复出现的另一件事，是你非常有效地制造 hype（热度），你也谈了一点，就是为一个想法制造 momentum。你有这个想法，让所有人 pitch 它，让所有人兴奋，然后它继续积累 hype 和 momentum。你团队里 maybe 的 Karl Jiang 说过一句："我觉得没有哪个 PM 曾让我对一个功能这么兴奋过。" Yuhki 说你通过制造 hype、并"hacking hype"——他是这么描述的——来克服人们的怀疑。聊聊这个，为什么你觉得它重要，你实际上是怎么做的。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: When you are spearheading an idea or a product, it's really on you to have a pulse on how everyone else is feeling about that product. And different products need different levels of excitement to make it out the door. If there is something that leadership has really strong conviction in, it's important for leadership to amp the whole company up behind that vision. On the flip side, if you yourself are pushing a zero to one idea from the bottoms up, the onus is even more on you to make sure that that project and that product is constantly propped up and that people are excited about it to make it out the door. And so one example is we've been talking about this product that I'm working on. And coming out of winter break this year, there's this sense, or at least I always suspect, that there's this sense of over winter break, everyone forgets what happened last year. It goes at the door because you were hopefully doing something that took your mind off work.
turns.zh: 当你在主导一个想法或产品时，真正取决于你，去感知其他人对那个产品的感受如何。不同的产品需要不同程度的兴奋度才能出得了门。如果有个东西是领导层有极强信念感的，那领导层有责任把整个公司都点燃、对准那个愿景。反过来，如果你自己是从下往上推一个从零到一的想法，那责任就更在你身上，要确保那个项目和产品被持续地撑起来、人们对它感到兴奋，才能出得了门。举一个例子：我们一直在谈我做的这个产品。今年冬假回来后，有种感觉——或者至少我总是怀疑——冬假期间，每个人都忘了去年发生了什么。它被关在门外，因为你希望做的是让你从工作中抽离的事。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so at the same time, there's this sense of how do you create forward momentum inside of a company in January when people are slowly coming back into office, everyone's trickling back in at different dates because everyone to click slightly different PTO, how do you rally people in a certain direction? And so we have this thing at Figma called SKO or Sales Kickoff, which is every year the sales team comes together, and we have a keynote and a set of fireside chats and stuff like that, and we talk about what's coming for the year. And at this point, our product, it existed, but it was absolutely barely built. It was rough around the edges. It had bugs every day. Maybe 10 people in the company were using it and something like that outside of the team.
turns.zh: 与此同时，就有这个问题：一月里，当大家慢慢回到办公室、每个人都因为 PTO 稍有不同而陆续回来时，你怎么在公司内部创造向前的 momentum？所以我们有个东西叫 SKO，也就是 Sales Kickoff（销售启动会），每年销售团队会聚在一起，我们有一场主题演讲和一系列炉边谈话等等，聊聊这一年要做什么。在那时，我们的产品已经存在，但绝对只是刚搭了个架子。它 edges 还很粗糙。每天都有 bug。可能公司里除了团队之外，只有 10 个人在用之类的。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, it was so important to me that this product got visibility in this forum because this was the first company-wide forum of the year where we were declaring priorities for the year. And so it was so important to me that this product had some sort of a moment, or speaking of show, don't tell, a demo in the context of this keynote. And so Kris, our CTO and Yuhki, our CPO, were giving this keynote on what does our year look like? And I really, really deeply insisted that we should include a demo. And I think what ended up happening is something like that, a demo that wasn't meant to be a demo or that people weren't expecting does so much in terms of driving that sense of hype and helping people see what you yourself see in the future. And what's really interesting is I think that hype is something that... You can't really create hype for something you don't believe in my opinion. The only way to create hype is to get people to see what you see.
turns.zh: 对，对我来说非常重要的一点是，这个产品要在这个论坛上获得曝光，因为这是这一年第一个全公司的论坛，我们要在其中宣告今年的重点。所以对我来说非常重要的是，这个产品要有某种"时刻"——或者说到"show, don't tell"，在这场主题演讲的情境里来一场 demo。我们的 CTO Kris 和 CPO Yuhki 在做一场关于"我们这一年长什么样"的主题演讲。我真的、真的、深深地坚持我们要加一段 demo。我觉得最终发生的是：一段本不打算做成 demo、或者人们没预期到的 demo，在驱动那种 hype 感、帮人们看见你自己在未来看到的东西方面，起了巨大的作用。很有意思的是，我觉得 hype 是种…… 你没法为你不相信的东西制造 hype，这是我的观点。制造 hype 的唯一方式，就是让人们看见你所看见的。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so I think that it's incredibly important to leverage very large forums like that Maker Week, like Sales Kickoff. We have CONFIG, which is our annual showcase to the world of what we're working on in order to get everyone to see what you're seeing and to be really scrappy about it and to really be the person who's pushing your product to its limits in the right moments. And I think what you find is that if you push your product to get visibility, maybe even beyond what the current stage of product development merits is that you have really incredible learnings because the more that you can put your product in front of people and get them to use it, the more signal you get on how it's trending. And so what ended up happening was something that could have originally been perceived as a distraction to the team actually ended up being something that added so much fuel to the fire in terms of, one, giving us product insights to inform our next steps. And two, getting the entire company to feel truly, deeply feel excited about getting this thing out the door.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，利用像 Maker Week、像 Sales Kickoff 这样非常大的论坛非常重要。我们有 CONFIG，这是我们每年向世界展示我们在做什么的盛会，目的是让所有人都看见你所看见的，并且真的要 scrappy（灵活将就）地去做，在正确的时刻真正成为那个把你的产品推向极限的人。我觉得你会发现，如果你把产品推到获得曝光——甚至可能是超越当前产品开发阶段所应得的曝光——你会得到非常了不起的学习，因为你把产品放到越多人面前、让他们去用，你得到的关于它走势的信号就越多。所以最终发生的是：一件本可能被视为团队分心的事，结果反而给火添了这么多燃料，一方面，给了我们从产品洞察来指导下一步的信息；另一方面，让整个公司真正、深深地感到兴奋，想要把这个东西做出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this pitch and product you're describing is the one that's going to be launching this mysterious new product, right?
turns.zh: 你描述的这个 pitch 和产品，就是要发布的那个神秘新产品的那个，对吧？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like we're going to build so much hype for this thing when it ever comes out. I'm so excited to learn what it is. Coming back to the point, so what I'm hearing essentially is you find it's important to take responsibility for this thing to become a thing at a company. A lot of people have an idea, they build a prototype, they build a hackathon project, and then they're like, "God, no one's ever doing anything with it. It's not going anywhere. Nothing ever happens." What I'm hearing is it's on you to get people excited about it and find these opportunities to get people excited about it. And there's also this, what I'm feeling is the feels is really important. It's like you have all the data probably. There's probably a logical case for this that you've made across the company, but what you're describing here is you need to get people hyped about it in a emotional, visceral way and basically find opportunities to do that is kind of a lesson here.
turns.zh: 我觉得等它真的出来的时候，我们会为这东西制造巨大的 hype。我超兴奋想知道它是什么。回到重点，所以我听到的本质上是：你觉得有责任让这个东西在公司里变成"一个东西"。很多人有个想法，做了原型，做了黑客马拉松项目，然后他们说"天，从来没人拿它干嘛。它哪儿也去不了。什么都没发生。" 我听到的是：让它发生是你的责任，让人们为它兴奋，并找到让人们兴奋的机会。还有一点，我感受到的是"feels"（感受）非常重要。就像你大概有了所有数据。你大概已经在全公司做过逻辑上的论证，但你在这里描述的是，你需要让人们以一种情绪的、visceral（本能的）方式对它 hype，并 basically 找到机会去做，这就是这里的 lesson。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: In my mind, there is internal hype, which is how do you get buy-in and everyone inside of the company to be fanging their fist on the table for a product to get built, but there's also external hype, which is like how do you get your users hyped about your product? How do you get them to really be so stoked when there are milestone occasions for your product or milestone launches and for them to be celebrating with you? And one of the things that I loved the most when I joined the company was Figma and design Twitter have had this very symbiotic relationship where each has grown with the other over time. And what really happens is anytime we launch something, you have all of design Twitter celebrating with us.
turns.zh: 在我脑海里，有内部的 hype——你怎么获得公司里每个人的认同、让他们为某个产品要被造出来而"捶桌子"；但也有外部的 hype——你怎么让你的用户对产品 hype？怎么让他们在你的产品有里程碑时刻、或里程碑式发布时，真的和你一起庆祝？我加入公司时最喜欢的一件事是，Figma 和设计 Twitter 之间有种非常共生（symbiotic）的关系，彼此随着时间一同成长。真正发生的是，每次我们发布东西，你都能看到整个设计 Twitter 和我们一起庆祝。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And one other moment when I thought it was very fun to drive hype was when I worked on FigJam in 2022. It was the one year FigJam anniversary in April, and project anniversaries or product anniversaries are quite an exciting milestone within the company. You bring everyone together, maybe you pop a bottle of champagne, you kind of celebrate how far you've come and what all you've learned since the launch. But we were really thinking like, "Okay, FigJam is awesome, but FigJam isn't just any product. Figjam has a personality. FigJam is cheeky. FigJam is fun. FigJam has this cute skeuomorphism going on where you feel like it's your friend. And so okay, how would you celebrate that moment for a friend?" You wouldn't really have an anniversary party. You would throw it a full on birthday party.
turns.zh: 另一个我觉得驱动 hype 很好玩的时刻，是 2022 年我在 FigJam 时。那是 FigJam 一周年纪念，在四月，项目周年或产品周年在公司内部是相当令人兴奋的里程碑。你把大家聚到一起，maybe 开瓶香槟，庆祝你走了多远、自发布以来学到了多少。但我们真的在想："好，FigJam 很棒，但 FigJam 不是普通的产品。FigJam 是有个性的。FigJam 是 cheeky（俏皮）的。FigJam 是有趣的。FigJam 有这种可爱的拟物（skeuomorphism）感，让你觉得它是你的朋友。那好，你会怎么为一个朋友庆祝那个时刻？" 你不会真的办个周年派对。你会给它办一场彻头彻尾的生日派对。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so what we basically did was at the one year anniversary of FigJam, I worked with the marketing team and our engineering team in order to basically kick off a mini launch inside of the product of a bunch of new features. And what we did was we Easter egged them through the product and each sort of product that we were releasing inside of FigJam was hidden under this little birthday present. And throughout the day, we sent all of our users on an Easter egg hunt of presents inside of FigJam. And so not only was a FigJam getting the presents, but it was our users getting the presents. I think that hype as well is really tied to emotion. So to the extent that a person using a product can feel like, "Oh, this thing that is built in the product was built for me not to advance the company's goals or anything like that, but to make me feel special, to make me feel happy."
turns.zh: 所以我们 basically 做的，是在 FigJam 一周年时，我和营销团队、工程团队一起，在产品的内部 basically 启动了一场迷你发布，发布一堆新功能。我们做的是把这些功能作为 Easter egg（彩蛋）藏在产品里，我们发布的每个 FigJam 里的产品，都藏在一个小生日礼物下面。一整天里，我们让所有用户去 FigJam 里进行一场"找礼物"的彩蛋 hunt。所以不仅 FigJam 收到了礼物，我们的用户也收到了礼物。我觉得那种 hype 也真的和情绪绑在一起。所以在用户使用产品时，能感觉到"哦，产品里 build 的这个东西是为我而做的，不是为了推进公司目标什么的，而是为了让我觉得特别、让我开心。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think that's a really key instrument in driving hype as well. And I think that something that's quite interesting about hype and getting your users to feel strongly about your product is that every product has their own brand of delight or excitement or energy. So hype for FigJam is incredibly different than hype from Figma, where hype for Figma might be this really, really niche design capability that unlocks this pain point that designers have been having for years and years. And then hype for Apple might be like the world's best unboxing experience or something like that. And so leaning into a product's brand in order to figure out what is the optimal way to generate hype with your audience and form that connection is something that's really important.
turns.zh: 我觉得那也是驱动 hype 的一个非常关键的手段。而且我觉得，让你的用户对你的产品有强烈感觉，这里面有件很有意思的事：每个产品都有自己的 delight、兴奋或能量的"品牌"。所以 FigJam 的 hype 和 Figma 的 hype 截然不同——Figma 的 hype 可能是某种非常、非常小众的设计能力，解锁了设计师多年来一直有的痛点。而 Apple 的 hype 可能是世界上最好的开箱体验之类的。所以，利用一个产品的品牌，去找出和你的受众制造 hype、并建立那种连接的最佳方式，是一件非常重要的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that example. Something else I'm finding as a thread throughout all of the lessons and stories he shares is just an immersion in your user base and truly knowing what they're excited about, what problems they have, and you talk about having strong conviction and painting a grand vision. It's one thing if someone that doesn't do that does that, it's just like, why would I believe them? Versus someone that like you, where you're just constantly talking to users and actually understand what they need. So I guess the question here is just what advice would you share with folks to build that, to be immersed with users? What do you actually do? How do you actually do that? Are you just organizing meetings, events? Are you scheduling chats? How do you do this?
turns.zh: 我超喜欢那个例子。我在你分享的所有教训和故事里发现的另一个 thread，就是沉浸在你的用户群里、真正知道他们兴奋什么、有什么问题，你谈到有强烈信念感、描绘宏大愿景。如果是一个不这么做的人去做这些，会像"我凭什么信他？" 而像你这样的人，你一直在和用户交谈、真的理解他们需要什么。所以问题来了：你会给大家什么建议，去建立那种沉浸、和用户在一起？你实际上怎么做？你是组织会议、活动吗？你安排聊天吗？你怎么做？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, so I think it honestly depends on the product. So when I worked at Meta, it was so easy. Everyone and their mom had opinion about the product, which was really great because it meant that anyone you met, you could kind of ask them what they liked, what they didn't like. You can relay that through the company, et cetera. Now at Figma, we have a slightly more niche audience. I think that hopefully, ultimately we get to everyone. We started with design teams, now we're thinking about the entire product development cycle and how we can build for that, and then who knows, beyond that could be anything. But I think that constantly immersing yourself in those circles where your users are is really important. So for me, it's like anytime that I'm catching up with a friend, who mildly works in tech or a tech adjacent field, I will generally be asking them about Figma. And I think what's really great is that as a company scales over time, their user base gets broader and broader. And so when we grew from a single product company with Figma into now a multi product company with FigJam, dev mode, etc, our audience exploded. And we already saw latent behavior inside of Figma, but now it's even more clear how wide reaching the product is. And so something that I find incredibly useful is to not just ask users of your product what they think about your product, but to ask non-users about your product, why they're not using your product. And actually I think that those are the most insightful conversations because I think that having a product shine and having a product do well and have great adoption isn't just about the product being great. It's also about the marketing and the perceptions that surround the product and potentially the hype that surrounds that, right?
turns.zh: 对，我觉得这 honestly 取决于产品。我在 Meta 时，那太容易了。每个人和他们的妈妈都对产品有意见，这真的很好，因为这意味着你遇到的任何人，你都可以问他们喜欢什么、不喜欢什么。你可以把这些在公司里传递，等等。现在在 Figma，我们的受众稍微小众一点。我希望最终我们能覆盖到所有人。我们从设计团队起步，现在我们在思考整个产品开发周期、以及我们怎么为它构建，然后谁知道呢，beyond 那可能是任何东西。但我觉得，持续沉浸在你的用户所在的那些圈子里，真的非常重要。对我来说，就是任何时候我和朋友叙旧，只要他稍微在科技或科技相关领域工作，我 generally 都会问他们关于 Figma 的事。我觉得很棒的是，随着公司随时间扩张，他们的用户群越来越广。当我们从只有 Figma 这一个产品的公司，变成现在有 FigJam、dev mode 等多个产品的公司，我们的受众爆炸式增长。我们已经在 Figma 里看到了 latent（潜在）行为，但现在更清楚产品覆盖有多广。所以我觉得非常有用的一点是：不只是问你产品的用户他们对产品怎么看，而是去问非用户他们对产品怎么看、为什么不用你的产品。其实我觉得那些是最有洞察的对话，因为我觉得，一个产品发光、做得好、有很高采用率，不只是产品很棒。也关乎围绕这个产品的营销、认知，可能还有围绕它的 hype，对吧？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so having those conversations about... I remember having an early conversation with folks from my previous team about, "Hey, are you guys using FigJam?" And they would be like, "Maybe sometimes." And I'd be like, "Well, why aren't you using FigJam? It's literally built for you." And then that led to a series of product insights that led us to invest in a set of features that would make it much easier for a non-designer to get started out on the canvas. So we launched this kind of placeholder experience that rather than traditional templates, really let people see the various use cases and preview the various use cases on the canvas. And so that was incredibly important. And then Figma, of course, is kind of like it's in this pro-sumer space where it's like you talk to anyone in tech and maybe they're your top total addressable market.
turns.zh: 所以有那些对话——我记得早先和我之前团队的人聊过"嘿，你们在用 FigJam 吗？" 他们会说"也许偶尔。" 我会说"那你为什么不用 FigJam？它简直就是为你们造的。" 然后这就引出了一系列产品洞察，让我们去投资一组功能，让非设计师更容易在画布上起步。所以我们推出了一种 placeholder 体验，不是传统的模板，而是真的让人们看到各种用例、并在画布上预览各种用例。这非常重要。而 Figma 当然处在一种 pro-sumer（专业消费者）的空间里，就像你跟科技圈任何人聊，maybe 他们就是你最大的总可寻址市场。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: But then there are some products I know that people work on which are very removed from the average person, you have infra products, security products and things like that, where you can't just walk up to someone and have a conversation with them about why aren't they using your product because that conversation might not make any sense. And so in those instances, I think that what's really important is it depends on the stage of company that you're at. If you're at an early stage company, you need to be the one going out there and having conversations with your users and just literally looking up your users through whatever channels necessary and figuring out how you can connect with them. I think this is also why founder market fit at startups is so important is because to the extent that you can use yourself as a limits test for what user needs there are, that helps you move really fast in the product development cycle.
turns.zh: 但也有些我知道人们做的产品，离普通人很远，比如基础设施产品、安全产品之类的，你没法直接走上去和人聊"你为什么不用你的产品"，因为那对话可能毫无意义。所以在那些情况下，我觉得非常重要的，是取决于你公司所处的阶段。如果你是早期公司，你需要自己去走出去、和用户对话，literally 通过各种必要渠道去找你的用户、想办法和他们建立连接。我觉得这也是为什么创始人与市场契合（founder market fit）在初创公司如此重要——因为在你能用自己作为用户需求的"limits test"的程度上，能帮你快速推进产品开发周期。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then if you're on the larger side, I think that having a really tight relationship with your sales team is really important. And basically, just being on sales calls because you want to be in a situation where the customer pain points on sales calls are cross pollinating into the product roadmap, and you also want to ensure that your sales team has visibility into what might be coming and are constantly informing that. And so I think really leaning into that, building that relationship between these traditionally more siloed orgs and hopping on those calls is something that I'd really recommend.
turns.zh: 而如果你在大一点的公司，我觉得和你的销售团队建立非常紧密的关系非常重要。basically，就是去旁听销售电话，因为你想要这样一种状态：销售电话上的客户痛点，能交叉授粉进产品路线图；你也要确保销售团队对你可能要推的东西有可见度，并不断给路线图提供信息。所以我觉得，真的去依靠这一点，在这些传统上更孤岛化的组织之间建立关系、并跳上那些电话，是我会强烈推荐的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Let's go actually one layer deeper here. So you're talking to people all the time about FigJam, "Aren't you using FigJam? What do you think of Figma? What do think of this?" You're hopping on sales calls. What do you do with what you hear? Is there kind of an operational approach where you... Do you just put in your head and sticks in your head and rolls around and comes up, things emerge? Do you have a place you put these insights, you're learning? Are you putting post-its in FigJam, for example. And then on the sales side, do you have a cadence where I'm going to join a sales call once a week, here's a person I love in sales, I'm going to try to join all the calls. How do you actually operationalize these things?
turns.zh: 太棒了。让我们再深一层。你一直在和用户聊 FigJam 的事——"你不用 FigJam 吗？你觉得 Figma 怎么样？你觉得这个怎么样？" 你跳上销售电话。你拿听到的东西做什么？有没有一种运营化的方法——你是就把它放脑子里、让它打转、然后东西自己冒出来？你有没有个地方放这些洞察、你学到的东西？你会把便利贴放 FigJam 里吗？在销售那边，你有没有个节奏，比如"我每周要参加一次销售电话，有个我喜欢的销售，我要尽量参加他所有的电话"？你实际上怎么把这些运营化？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: The insights get operationalized in a number of ways. So first is... So yeah, let's continue using FigJam as an example. I think, like I mentioned, Figma as a company uses FigJam for everything. Multiple FigJam files are made per day, per meeting, et cetera. We had this initial situation where people outside of the company were mostly using FigJam for brainstorms. And so as we were scaling our FigJam sales team, I sort of set up a recurring cadence with the folks in our sales team in order to understand like, "Okay, what are you guys hearing?" And then I would share what was coming, and then I would use their input as signal as to what should be prioritized or deprioritized on the roadmap. And they would use my signal to understand what were the various use cases that they could be pushing with the customers.
turns.zh: 这些洞察以好几种方式被运营化。首先——我们继续用 FigJam 当例子。就像我提到的，Figma 作为一家公司，所有事都用 FigJam。每天、每场会议都会建多个 FigJam 文件，等等。我们最初的情况是，公司外的人大多用 FigJam 做头脑风暴。所以随着我们扩展 FigJam 销售团队，我和销售团队的同事建立了一个 recurring（定期）的节奏，去了解"好，你们听到了什么？" 然后我会分享将要推的东西，再用他们的输入作为信号，来判断路线图该优先什么、或降级什么。而他们会用我的信号，去理解他们可以向客户推的各种用例。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And one thing that happened during one of the meetings was I literally walked them through, this meeting, this is how I use FigJam. In this meeting, this is how I use FigJam. In this meeting, this is how I use FigJam, blah, blah, blah. And what that resulted in was I actually made a Loom video walking through my weekend FigJam, that our sales team later distributed to a bunch of companies to inspire them as to like, "Hey, not only can you use FigJam for this, you can use Fig Jam for X, Y, Z. You can use it for your team pickups. You can use it for your retros. You can use it for planning your mom's birthday party. You can use it for planning your all hands. You can use it for sketching out the contents of what's going to go into your next deck," so on and so forth. And so it basically manifests in two way, the first is having it inform the prioritization of your product roadmap.
turns.zh: 其中一次会议发生的一件事是，我 literally 带着他们过了一遍：这场会议，我是这么用 FigJam 的；那场会议，我是这么用的；这场会议，我是这么用的，blah blah blah。结果是，我 actually 做了一段 Loom 视频，walk through 我的周末 FigJam，后来我们的销售团队把它分发给很多公司，去启发他们："嘿，你不仅能用 FigJam 做这个，你还能用 FigJam 做 X、Y、Z。你能用它做团队 pickup。你能用它做 retro。你能用它策划你妈的生日派对。你能用它策划全员大会。你能用它草拟你下一份 deck 的内容，" 等等等等。所以它 basically 以两种方式呈现：一是让它为你的产品路线图优先级提供信息。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then the second is what ideally creating artifacts that the sales team can use to evangelize the things that you are seeing and the stepping stones to that vision that you creating. And then the last thing is that sometimes the conversations aren't immediately actionable, right? Sometimes the sales team has an insight or has a request that is just objectively not feasible because the team has too much on its plate. Conversely, sometimes the team might have a suggestion for something that might be pitched to sales folks that's too early given the stage of the conversation. And for that, we basically have... We store it in Asana basically. We have this integration, which many companies might have, which is like Slack integration, where you can react with an Asana emoji, and then any piece of feedback that comes in from sales or from the rest of the company gets turned into a task in your backlog, and then you do a weekly grooming of that.
turns.zh: 二是，理想情况下，创造出销售团队能用来"传福音"的工件，去传播他们看到的、以及通往你正在创造的那个愿景的踏脚石。最后一点是，有时这些对话不是立刻可行动的，对吧？有时销售团队有个洞察或请求，客观上就是不可行，因为团队盘子已经太满了。反过来，有时团队可能有个建议，可以 pitch 给销售同事，但就对话所处的阶段来说太早了。对此，我们 basically 有…… 我们 basically 把它存在 Asana 里。我们有个集成——很多公司可能也有——就是 Slack 集成，你可以 react 一个 Asana 表情，然后任何来自销售或公司其他地方的反馈，都会变成一个 backlog 里的任务，然后你每周做一轮 grooming。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Cool. Very tactical and useful.
turns.zh: 太棒了。酷。非常具体、有用。
