turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another thread that I've noticed, and I wasn't planning to go in this direction, but you just care so deeply about the things you work on. You actually really, really love it and want it to be incredibly successful and feels like you're just always thinking about it. Reminding me of this quote from your colleague Karl, they shared that, "It feels like you care deeply, which makes me care deeply. Who wants to be led by someone who doesn't care about what they're building?" It feels like that's an important part of the way you work and think. Is there anything you want to say about that?
turns.zh: 我注意到的另一个 thread，我本来没打算往这个方向走，但你对你做的事真的非常、非常在乎。你真的、真的很爱它，想让它极其成功，感觉你一直在想它。让我想起你同事 Karl 分享的一句引语："感觉你 deeply 在乎，这让我也 deeply 在乎。谁想被一个不在乎自己正在 build 什么的人领导？" 感觉那是你工作和思维方式中重要的一部分。你想对此说点什么吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: When I started out my product career, I actually-
turns.zh: 当我刚开始我的产品生涯时，我 actually——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... About that.
turns.zh: ……关于那个。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: When I started out my product career, I actually joined as a RPM, or rotational product manager, at Meta, which was effectively a program that brought together new grad PMs, so people who had zero PM experience and taught them how to be PMs. And, in the beginning of this program, we had a series of conversations with leaders across the company. And, one particularly notable conversation was with Julie Zhu, who was the first ever intern at Meta and the VP of design. And, she was giving us feedback and advice about how to draft compelling product strategy, etc. And, something she said that has stuck with me throughout my entire product career is that when two people disagree about product strategy, it is because they have different assumptions. Because, if you have the same assumptions, there is no reason why a person should think, "We should do X versus we should do Y." And so, it's like, "Okay, how does this relate to what you were just asking about feeling deeply and caring about what you're building?"
turns.zh: 当我刚开始我的产品生涯时，我 actually 是以 RPM（轮岗产品经理）的身份加入 Meta 的，这 basically 是一个把新毕业的 PM——也就是零 PM 经验的人——聚在一起、教他们怎么做 PM 的项目。在这个项目开始时，我们和全公司的很多领导者做了一系列对话。其中一次特别值得注意的，是和 Julie Zhu 的对话，她是 Meta 的第一位实习生、也是设计副总裁。她给了我们关于如何起草有说服力的产品战略等反馈和建议。有句话让我整个产品生涯都记着：当两个人在产品战略上意见不合时，是因为他们有不同的假设。因为如果假设相同，就没有理由一个人会想"我们应该做 X 而不是 Y"。所以，这跟刚刚你问的"深切感受、在乎你正在 build 的东西"有什么关系？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think that it's really important to not just build a roadmap because it's handed to you, or not just build an idea because it's handed to you. I think that you need to understand in the event that it's a top-down strategy, what are the assumptions that led to folks believing that that is the right idea? And then, if it is you pushing something bottoms up, you need to be able to ensure that everyone else has the same assumptions that you have in your head that leads them to believe deeply or not believe deeply. And I think what's really important is that people can, to Carl's point, gauge someone is about a project. And, my take is that, the more you believe in an idea, the more natural it is to be passionate about it.
turns.zh: 我觉得，很重要的一点是，不要只是因为路线图是交给你的、或者一个想法是交给你的，就去 build 它。我觉得，你需要去理解——如果这是一个自上而下的战略——导致人们相信那是对的想法的那些假设是什么？然后，如果是你自下而上在推某个东西，你需要能确保其他人和你脑子里有同样的假设，那些假设让他们深切相信、或不相信。我觉得非常重要的一点是，人们，借用 Carl 的话，能 gauge（衡量）一个人对一个项目的在乎程度。而我的看法是，你越相信一个想法，对它充满热情就越自然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine people listening to this will feel like, "Oh shit, I don't really love what I'm working on. I don't work at Figma. I don't have the best of most amazing products." Maybe it's hard to get excited about stuff. Is there anything you could share there? Just say you're working on something that you're not so passionate about, is it a fine thing, keep searching, or is it just figure out something you're excited about? Any advice there for someone in that boat?
turns.zh: 我想象听这个的人会觉得"哦糟了，我其实不爱我正在做的事。我不在 Figma 工作。我没有最棒、最惊人的产品。" 也许很难对东西感到兴奋。你能在那方面分享点什么吗？就说你正在做一个你没那么热情的事，这是正常的吗、继续找，还是就说去找到你兴奋的东西？对处于那种境地的人的建议？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: My first piece of advice would be to not just think about the scope of what you are working on as the thing that happens to be in flight at any given moment. But, if you're working in a company, take a step back, understand the vision of that company, and understand your users, and understand if there's anything in that space that you are passionate about. I think it's quite easy to believe that the project that you're working on is your scope. My take is that your scope is the world, and to the extent that you can figure out does the idea that you're passionate about fall within your company, versus fall outside of your company, that should guide the next steps in your career. And so, I think that potentially common misconception is that founding something is just for capital F founders, but I think that anyone can found something. You can found something inside of an existing company, you can found something from scratch. And, there are different reasons why you would do each, right?
turns.zh: 我的第一个建议是，不要只把你正在做的东西的"scope"当成恰好此刻在飞的那件事。但如果你在一家公司，退一步，理解那家公司的愿景，理解你的用户，并理解在那个空间里有没有什么是你充满热情的。我觉得很容易相信你正在做的项目就是你的 scope。我的看法是，你的 scope 就是世界，在你能弄清楚"你充满热情的想法是在公司内、还是公司外"的程度上，那应该指导你职业的下一步。所以我觉得，一个常见的误解是，创办东西只是大写 F 的 founders（创始人）的事，但我觉得任何人都可以创办东西。你可以在一家现有公司里创办东西，你也可以从零创办东西。而做每一种，理由都不同，对吧？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: The reasons why you would found inside of an existing company is if you think that there is a distribution advantage that you want to take advantage of, if there is a technical or platform advantage that you want to take advantage of. Or, there's also a reality which is it's slightly less risk. So, depending on what your risk tolerance is, you can figure out what makes sense. There are things that are harder inside of an existing company, right? It's harder to take an executive decision. You actually cannot take an executive decision. You need to receive buy-in on every single decision that you make. Sometimes it's harder to move faster. And then sometimes, there are things that are just different when you're starting inside of an existing company, versus starting something outright.
turns.zh: 你在现有公司里创办的理由是：如果你觉得有想利用的分发优势，或者有想利用的技术或平台优势。还有一个现实是，它的风险稍微小一点。所以，取决于你的风险偏好，你可以判断什么合理。在现有公司里，有些事更难，对吧？更难做高管层的决策。你 actually 不能做高管决策。你做的每一个决策都需要获得认同。有时更难更快推进。然后有时，在现有公司里起步和 outright（直接）从零起步，就是有些东西不一样。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So the things that are different is building a team is quite different. The way that you recruit and the set of folks that you can recruit from, that composition is quite different. And then, the way that you pitch and who you are pitching to is quite different. And so, I think that sometimes, yeah, it makes sense to found inside of a company and to use that to make your flame burn, right? Sometimes it makes sense to found outright. But I think that the first key to being passionate about what you're working on is to find an idea that you're passionate about.
turns.zh: 所以不一样的地方是：建团队相当不同。你招募的方式、你能招募的那群人，构成相当不同。然后，你做 pitch 的对象、以及你 pitch 给谁，也相当不同。所以我觉得，有时在公司内部创办、用它来让你的火焰燃烧，是有道理的，对吧？有时 outright 从零创办是有道理的。但我觉得，对你正在做的事充满热情的第一关键，是找到一个你充满热情的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this as a metaphor of the flame where it applies both to you as a person at a company and keeping that flame going and building it. And then also the idea and a project that accompanies little flame that you're growing over time, building momentum around. So you've hinted at this whole idea of starting zero to one and building new products within larger companies, which I want to get to. We've gone really deep on a bunch of awesome stuff and I'm really happy we did. There's four more skills of things you're amazing at. So here's an idea, let me share the four. How about you pick two that you're most passionate about that you think you have the most advice to share, and then we'll just do those, and then we'll go to what you've learned about building something completely new at a larger company? How does that sound?
turns.zh: 我超喜欢这个"火焰"的比喻，它既适用于你作为一家公司的个人、去保持那团火燃烧并壮大它，也适用于那个想法、以及随它而来的、你随时间培育的小火焰、在它周围建立 momentum。所以你 hinted at 这整个"从零到一、在更大的公司里打造新产品"的想法，这个我想接下来聊。我们已经就一堆很棒的东西聊得很深了，我很高兴我们这么做了。你超厉害的技能还有四个。所以这是想法，让我分享这四个。你挑两个你最充满热情、觉得最有建议可分享的，然后我们就做那两个，然后我们再聊你在"在更大的公司里从零打造全新东西"中学到的？听起来怎么样？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, from folks that you work with, the four other skills, things you're amazing at, and I still want to hear the things you think you're not amazing at. One is creativity, that you have really creative solutions to problems. Two is empathy. You're really strong at empathizing with users and using that to build amazing products. Three is culture. Sho tells me you're the culture carrier at Figma, which is amazing, because the culture there from what I hear is amazing. And then, four is dealing with change. You're amazing at just like, "Okay, cool. Priorities are changing. Great, let's go. Here we go." Which of those two feel most interesting to you?
turns.zh: 好。从我共事的人那里，另外四个技能、你超厉害的事——而且我还是想听你觉得你不那么厉害的事。一个是创造力，你对问题有非常有创意的解决方案。二是同理心。你非常擅长对用户共情、并用它打造了不起的产品。三是文化。Sho 告诉我你是 Figma 的"文化担当"（culture carrier），这很了不起，因为据我所闻那里的文化超棒。四是应对变化。你就超擅长"好，酷。优先级在变。太好了，走。来了。" 那两个对你来说最有趣？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Maybe we can do the latter two, because they're a little bit different than the other things we've been discussing. Yeah.
turns.zh: 也许我们可以做后两个，因为它们和我们之前讨论的有点不一样。好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds great. So, I guess culture. Let me start there. Okay, so yeah, Sho called you the culture carrier Figma. I hear there's some fun things you all do there. There's something called the hot seat, there's something called the Figgies. First of all, can you maybe explain these two things? And then just broadly, what you find is important about focusing on culture as a PM?
turns.zh: 听起来很棒。那，我猜是文化。我从那里开始。好，所以是的，Sho 叫你 Figma 的"文化担当"。我听说你们在那儿有些好玩的事。有个叫 hot seat（热座）的，有个叫 Figgies 的。首先，你能解释一下这两件事吗？然后 broadly，作为 PM 你为什么觉得关注文化很重要？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, I can definitely talk about those two things. So, hot seat is actually a tradition I started at our first PM offsite post-pandemic. So this was March of 2022. The PM team was sub-15 people at that point, and we all fit around a dinner table, which is no longer true today. And, it was really important to me that we all got to know each other in a context that was outside of work. I think that PMing is a highly collaborative function. And, to the extent that you have great relationships with all the teams that you're interfacing with, one is it goes a long way in terms of the product, but two, speaking about passion, it makes your day-to-day so much more fun if you feel like you're working with your friends, and if you are working with your friends.
turns.zh: 对，这两件事我 definitely 能聊。hot seat 其实是我疫情后第一次 PM offsite 时发起的一个传统。那是 2022 年三月。那时 PM 团队不到 15 人，我们全部能围坐在一张餐桌旁，今天已经不是这样了。对我来说非常重要的一点是，我们要在一个工作之外的情境里互相了解。我觉得 PM 是一个高度协作的职能。在你能和所有你对接的团队建立好关系的程度上，一来对产品大有帮助，二来，说到热情，如果你觉得是在和朋友一起工作、如果你真的和朋友一起工作，你的日常会快乐得多。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, we were coming out of a long intense day session, and I was thinking about, "Okay, how do we break the ice?" And, hot seat is this game where you go around the table and each person gets two minutes on the clock and everyone else at the table can ask them anything. And if they want to, they can decline to answer. But we try and keep it, generally speaking, quite friendly and comfortable for folks. And so, we kicked off this game. And, what was really interesting was earlier that day we had done a personality test, as a side note, our PM team is obsessed with personality tests.
turns.zh: 所以，我们刚结束漫长 intense 的一天会议，我在想"好，我们怎么破冰？" 而 hot seat 是一个游戏，大家围桌转一圈，每个人有两分钟倒计时，桌上其他人可以问他们任何问题。如果他们愿意，可以拒绝回答。但我们尽量让它总体保持相当友好、让人舒服。我们就开启了这个游戏。很有意思的是，那天早些时候我们做了一个性格测试——顺便说，我们的 PM 团队对性格测试很着迷。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which personality test, by the way?
turns.zh: 顺便问，哪个性格测试？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: We to this day say the best one was the one that we did at this offsite, which is the Strengths Finder test. And, what had basically happened was over the course of that morning, we had all dug into... We were saying, "What are our strengths? What are our weaknesses?" Etc. And we had this really fun foundation to build on during the game of hot seat, where it was like, we were digging into like, "What about people's backgrounds made them think the way that they do today? And, what random anecdote at age seven of playing catch with their dad in the field led to how they thought about auto layout? Blah, blah, blah, blah." And, I think that being able to understand what motivates a person is so important when you're working with them, and also just in building a connection with them. And so, that was this moment that really brought the whole team together.
turns.zh: 我们至今说最好的是在这次 offsite 上做的那个，叫 Strengths Finder（优势识别器）测试。那天上午，我们 basically 都深挖了…… 我们在说"我们的优势是什么？我们的弱项是什么？" 等等。我们在 hot seat 游戏时有了一个非常有趣的基础可以建立，就像我们在挖"人们的什么背景让他们有今天的思维方式？一个七岁时和爸爸在田野里玩接球时的什么 random 软事，导致了他怎么想 auto layout？blah blah blah blah。" 我觉得，理解什么在激励一个人，在你和他共事时非常重要，而且在和他建立连接上也很重要。所以，那是真正把整个团队凝聚在一起的时刻。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Something that I was really gratified to hear after is that, since then, hot seat has become a tradition within the company. And so, all the PMs went on to play it with their own teams. Yuki and Sho went on to play it with the exec team, so on and so forth. And so, it's become this thing that now anytime that someone joins the team, okay, you put them in the hot seat. And then, if you're meeting someone's significant other, you put them in the hot seat. And it's this thing that is just totally spread, but it's a really fun way to just get to know folks and what drives them. So, that's one of my favorites. I highly recommend.
turns.zh: 之后我真的很有成就感地听到，从那以后，hot seat 成了公司里的一个传统。所以，所有 PM 都接着在自己的团队里玩它。Yuki 和 Sho 接着在 exec 团队里玩它，等等等等。所以，它变成了这样一件事：现在任何时候有人加入团队，好，你把他放进 hot seat。然后，如果你见到某人的另一半，你把他放进 hot seat。它就是这样完全传开了，但它真的是一种超好玩的了解大家、以及是什么驱动他们的方式。所以，这是我最喜欢的之一。我强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: The second thing that you asked about, which was the Figgies. And, this is basically an Oscar style awards ceremony that was hacked together. And so, where the Figgies was inspired from was actually every year we have... I was mentioning like SKO, our sales kickoff. And, on the last night of SKO, there's this award ceremony, where they appreciate all of the incredible work that has taken place in the sales and marketing org. And I saw this and I was like, "This is incredible. We should absolutely be celebrating the product team as well when we're together." And so, what I did was I basically took our Figma boardroom, which is called Bigma, and worked with another PM Elan to deck it out, and a red carpet, gold curtains, etc. And we bought little Oscar trophies for everyone, and got their names written on it, and voted people in for all of these absurd categories, like most likely to name their child Figma, most likely to go their career without writing a PRD. Blah, blah, blah.
turns.zh: 你问的第二件事，是 Figgies。这 basically 是一个被 hack 出来的奥斯卡风格颁奖典礼。Figgies 的灵感来源其实是：每年我们都有…… 我之前提到的 SKO，我们的销售启动会。在 SKO 最后一晚，有一场颁奖典礼，表彰销售和营销组织里发生的所有了不起的工作。我看到这个，就想"这太了不起了。我们也绝对应该在聚在一起时，庆祝产品团队。" 所以，我 basically 拿了我们叫 Bigma 的 Figma 会议室，和另一个 PM Elan 一起把它布置起来，铺红毯、挂金色窗帘等等。我们给每个人买了小奥斯卡奖杯，把他们的名字写上，并按各种荒唐的类别给人投票，比如"最有可能给孩子起名叫 Figma"、"最有可能整个职业生涯都不写一篇 PRD"。blah blah blah。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And, of course, forced everyone to give some acceptance speech. But, I think that making people feel appreciated for even just the quirks and the energy that they bring to the team is something that's incredibly important. And celebrating that diversity together is something that I think goes a long way in terms of making people feel close, and also making people understand maybe someone who they don't know that well on the PM team, because then you learn, "Okay, beyond them having this Zoom background, this is what's cheeky about them. Or this is what's interesting or unique about them." And so, I think that culture is so important. Figma has this core value called play, which I love, which really emphasizes just that everyone should be having fun at all times, and work should be fun, and gathering should be fun. And I think that I personally am a huge believer in this remote first role that we live in, you also want to take advantage of those times when you're able to get together and do things that make the team feel geographically close, even when they're geographically spread out.
turns.zh: 当然，还逼着每个人发表获奖感言。但我觉得，让人们即使只是为他们给团队带来的那些怪癖和能量而感到被欣赏，是极其重要的事。一起庆祝那种多样性，在让人们感到亲近、也让他们了解 PM 团队里某个不太熟的人方面，大有裨益，因为你然后会知道"好，除了他们有那个 Zoom 背景，这就是他们俏皮的地方。或者这就是他们有趣或独特的地方。" 所以我觉得文化非常重要。Figma 有一个核心价值叫 play（玩），我很喜欢，它真的强调每个人应该时刻在玩、工作应该好玩、聚会应该好玩。我个人非常相信这种我们所处的 remote first（远程优先）角色，你也要利用那些能把大家聚到一起、做让团队感到地理上亲近的事情的时机，即使他们在地理上是分散的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man, it's so fun. And I love that it's just like, you did this, right? It's not like Dylan is adding all these rituals to the team. It's very bottom up. And, in theory, any PM on the team could have done this.
turns.zh: 哦天，太好玩了。而且我超喜欢它就像——是你做的，对吧？不是 Dylan 往团队里加所有这些仪式。它是非常自下而上的。而理论上，团队里任何 PM 都可能做这件事。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: It's interesting, something that I had heard, Vishal Shah, who was the former head of product at Instagram say, is that, often in companies culture is set top down, and then the innovation that comes out of that is bottoms up. And so, I think in the first place, having a value like play does a lot in order to make folks feel like these things are celebrated and time should be carved out for them.
turns.zh: 有个我听到过的有意思的事，Vishal Shah——Instagram 前产品负责人——说过：往往在公司里，文化是自上而下设定的，而从那里面出来的创新是自下而上的。所以我觉得，首先，拥有一个像 play 这样的价值，在让人们觉得这些事被庆祝、应该为其留出时间方面，作用很大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To come back to your original point of just culture is everything, a lot of PMs are like, "I have so much work to do. I have so many things to do. I'm just working all day every day." What can you tell them about why this is so important and worth putting some time into? And should everybody? Or is it just like, "If you're excited about this, do it. If not, don't worry"?
turns.zh: 回到你最初的观点——文化就是一切——很多 PM 是"我有这么多工作要做。我有这么多事。我每天都干活。" 你能告诉他们，为什么这如此重要、值得投入点时间？是每个人都该做吗？还是就像"如果你对这兴奋，就做。不兴奋，别担心"？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think culture is important in that it establishes trust between groups of people. And so, I think that actually earlier you were asking about passion and what makes someone feel passionate about work. And I think realistically, that passion breaks down into two things. One is, are you passionate about the vision that you're building towards? Which we spoke about. But the second thing is, are you passionate about the people who you work with?
turns.zh: 我觉得文化重要，是因为它在人群之间建立信任。所以，其实早些时候你在问热情、以及什么让一个人对工作有热情。而我觉得现实地看，那种热情可拆成两件事。一是，你对你要构建的那个愿景有热情吗？这个我们聊过。但第二件事是，你对和你共事的人有热情吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And, I think that roadmaps change, products change, but feeling a connection to the folks that you're working with make you much more durable as a team. It means that when times get tough, which they will, your gut instinct is to rally together and collaborate together to find a solution, rather than to jump ship or something. I think personally, I'm in love with my team. They give me so much joy and happiness on a daily basis. I was telling them the other day that when they post prototypes in our Slack channel, sometimes I get little flutters in my chest like when you have a crush on someone. And, I think that having that emotional connection to your team is fun. And I think that emotional connection comes from investing in culture.
turns.zh: 而且，我觉得路线图会变、产品会变，但和你共事的人之间的连接感，会让你们作为一个团队更持久。这意味着当艰难时刻到来——它一定会来——你的本能是团结在一起、协作找出解决方案，而不是跳船什么的。就我个人而言，我爱死我的团队了。他们每天给我那么多快乐和幸福。前几天我告诉他们，当他们在我们 Slack 频道里发原型时，有时我胸口会小鹿乱撞，就像你对某人有 crush 时那样。我觉得和团队有那种情感连接很有趣。而我觉得那种情感连接，来自对文化的投入。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, it's like, you did it. You made it happen, right? It's not like, "Oh, this sucks. My team's no fun." It's like, you can make it more fun. And I think the two examples you shared are awesome, because one is a high-end version where there's a lot of work. And the hot seat, it's just a quick idea that takes no work, just an idea, and then you just ask to do it, and it's there.
turns.zh: 再说一次，就像——是你做的。你让它发生了，对吧？不是"哦，这糟透了。我的团队不好玩。" 而是"你能让它更好玩。" 我觉得你分享的两个例子超棒，因为一个是要花很多功夫的高端版本。而 hot seat，只是一个不费功夫的小点子、一个想法，你只要提议做、它就在那儿了。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Okay, so actually, I want to combat the perception that the Figgy's was a high production, high cost thing. It was very low cost. I ordered everything on Amazon and assembled it in an hour. And so, there are ways to be scrappy in making things come together. And so, I would say, don't be intimidated by any idea of being too large to take on. Just go for it.
turns.zh: 好，其实我想反驳一下"Figgies 是个高制作、高成本的东西"这种认知。它成本非常低。我所有东西都在 Amazon 上订，用一小时组装好。所以，在把东西凑到一起这件事上，是有办法 scrappy 的。所以我想说，别被"任何想法都太大、扛不动"吓到。直接去做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome correction. Okay, final trait you're great at. Somebody shared that you pivot with grace and enthusiasm when things change and priorities change, projects are killed, projects are spun up. There's something that a lot of people at companies just get so sad about, "Oh my God, things keep changing. My project's killed. Oh, this priority changed." It feels like you've learned to make that a superpower. What can you share about what you've learned there and how to leverage that into doing great and being successful?
turns.zh: 这是个超棒的纠正。好，你超厉害的最后一个特质。有人分享说，当事情变化、优先级变化、项目被砍、项目被启动，你能优雅而热情地 pivot。很多公司里的人就为这种事特别难过："哦我的天，事情一直在变。我的项目被砍了。哦，这个优先级变了。" 看起来你学会了把那变成一种超能力。你能分享一下你在那方面学到的、以及怎么利用它去做出成绩、走向成功？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: For this one, I could actually maybe give an example that preceded my product career, which was, when I was in college, I actually founded a national design conference for students across the country. And the way that this came about was when I was in college, design was very much having a watershed moment in tech. So, companies like Airbnb and Pinterest were leading an industry and they were leading not just because they built technology and made it accessible, but because they were really using the interface layer to differentiate. So there was this point where software had reached a certain level of saturation, where things that were not possible were now suddenly possible, and now suddenly possible in multiple companies. And design became this differentiator, which is really exciting. But at the same time, none of this was reflected in most schools across the country.
turns.zh: 关于这个，我也许能举一个早于我产品生涯的例子。我上大学时，actually 为全国各地学生创办了一个全国性的设计大会。它的由来是：我上大学时，设计在科技界正经历一个分水岭时刻。像 Airbnb 和 Pinterest 这样的公司正在引领一个行业，它们引领不只是因为构建了技术、让它可用，更因为它们真的在用界面层来做差异化。所以有这么一个点：软件达到了某种饱和程度，原本不可能的事突然可能了，而现在突然多家公司都可能了。设计成了一种差异化因素，这真的令人兴奋。但与此同时，全国大多数学校里，这一点都没有被反映出来。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, I went to Princeton and there was nothing that resembled product design in our curriculum. And this was baffling to me, because I was like, "There is such clear momentum..." Speaking about momentum in industry about this being a profession that is so important and so influential in building the next generation of companies. Yet, the groundwork to make that happen wasn't really there. And then, I interned at Facebook, and I realized that my entire class of 25 interns had very similar experiences, where they too were self-taught product designers. And so, that summer, I actually watched a documentary that was coincidentally produced by Envision that featured folks like John Maeda, amongst others, and was talking about how design changed the world that we lived in, and was going to rewrite the future, which I really believed in. And so, I was incentivized to found this conference called Design Nation that would democratize access to a design education and bring together top students from across the country with industry leaders.
turns.zh: 我去了 Princeton，我们的课程里没有任何像产品设计的东西。这让我 baffling（困惑），因为我就想"有这么清晰的 momentum"——说到行业里的 momentum——关于这是一个如此重要、在构建下一代公司方面如此有影响力的职业。然而，让那发生的基础工作却并不在那儿。然后，我在 Facebook 实习，我意识到我的整个 25 人实习班都有非常相似的经历，他们也都是自学成才的产品设计师。所以那年夏天，我 actually 看了一部巧合由 Envision 制作的纪录片，里面有 John Maeda 等人，讲的是设计如何改变了我们生活的世界、并将重写未来，我真的相信这一点。所以，我被激励去创办这个叫 Design Nation 的大会，它会让设计教育的获取民主化，把全国顶尖学生和行业领袖聚到一起。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And originally, my plan was to build this within an organization that already existed at Princeton, because they had the funding, they had the resources, they had the expertise in order to make this a reality. And then, what actually ended up happening was they too were skeptical of the business value of design and didn't think it would be possible for something like this to be funded. And so, I went from building something in a situation where I thought finances, expenditures, connections, et cetera, were totally taken care of, to having none of that and needing to build it from the ground up.
turns.zh: 最初，我的计划是在 Princeton 一个已经存在的组织内部 build 它，因为他们有资金、有资源、有专业知识，能让它成真。然后真正发生的是，他们也对设计商业价值持怀疑态度，觉得这种事不可能被资助。所以我从一个"财务、支出、人脉等等都完全有人管"的情况，变成了什么都没有、需要从零 build。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And, it was funny, one of the best pieces of advice I got in college was, don't underestimate the power for .edu email address. And I just went on a spree, cold emailing so many people, so many executives about this problem that I was trying to solve. And, what actually ended up happening was people would hop on the phone with me, and a lot of the folks who I spoke to, designers who I really admire, like Daniel Burke, Jamie [inaudible 01:10:46], et cetera, were folks who would be like, "Oh my God, this was such a problem when I was in college. Of course I'll help you solve it. I can't believe it hasn't been solved yet."
turns.zh: 而且，好玩的是，大学时我得到的最好建议之一是：别低估 .edu 邮箱地址的力量。我就开启了一场狂潮，cold emailing 好多好多人、好多高管，聊我试图解决的这个问题。真正发生的是，人们会和我通电话，而我聊过的很多人——我真的很钦佩的设计师，像 Daniel Burke、Jamie [inaudible 01:10:46] 等等——都会像"哦我的天，我上大学时这也是个大问题。我当然帮你解决它。我不敢相信它还没被解决。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, ultimately, it grew into this conference that lasted many years, brought together folks from originally around the country, then more recently around the world. And ultimately, did live under that broader organization. But I think, having the ability to, in the absence of formal backing or something, still chase after something and maybe pivot the way that you're thinking about it, or pivot the way that you are allocating your own time. Maybe suddenly speakers is not the most important thing, fundraising is the most important thing. Or, building a hype landing page so that you seem more legit than a very scrappy few-person student organization is the most important thing. And just being quite adaptable when it comes to resourcing, I think is very important.
turns.zh: 所以最终，它成长为一个持续多年的大会，最初把全国各地的人聚到一起，后来更近是全世界的人。最终，它确实归到了那个更大的组织之下。但我觉得，在缺乏正式支持的情况下，依然去追逐某件事、也许调整你思考它的方式、或者调整你分配自己时间的方式，这种能力很重要。也许突然之间，演讲者不是最重要的，筹款才是最重要的。或者，建一个 hype 落地页、让你看起来比一个非常 scrappy 的几人学生组织更 legit，才是最重要的。在资源配置上相当 adapt（适应），我觉得非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. It shows another trait, Mahika, in our archeological study, which has come up a bunch, and I'm just putting my finger on it, is just high agency. It feels like you're just consistently just like, "I'll make this happen myself. This problem exists. We need more product designers in school. I will solve that problem." And I love that. And by the way, Design Nation for folks that want to explore that, how do they find that? And it's still going, right?
turns.zh: 那是个超棒的例子。它展示了另一个特质，Mahika，在我们的考古研究里反复出现、而我正把它指出来，就是高能动性（high agency）。感觉你 consistently 就是"我自己让这事发生。这个问题存在。我们需要学校里有更多产品设计师。我会解决那个问题。" 我爱这点。顺便，想探索 Design Nation 的人，怎么找到它？而且它还在继续，对吧？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah. So, you can Google Design Nation.
turns.zh: 对。你可以 Google Design Nation。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And, we have a Instagram page amongst other things. And, yeah, last year we had folks like Stuart Weitzman and Joe Gebbia, who's one of the co-founders of Airbnb come and speak, which was super exciting.
turns.zh: 我们有 Instagram 页面等等。去年我们有像 Stuart Weitzman、Joe Gebbia（Airbnb 联合创始人之一）这样的人来演讲，超令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And then, who is it for? It's for students? People in college that want to learn to be designers?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那，它是给谁的？给学生？想学做设计师的大学生？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, it's for design-driven college students. I think one thing to call out is that one of my focuses in the early years was to ensure that this is for, not just capital D designers, but design driven students. So, we also took engineers who are very design minded and marketers who are very design minded, et cetera, because of that core belief that the most innovative solutions will come out of people that are operating at this intersectionality.
turns.zh: 对，是给有设计驱动力的大学生的。我觉得有一点要说明：我早年的一个重点是，确保这不只是给大写 D 的设计师，而是给有设计驱动力的学生。所以我们也收了非常有设计思维工程师、非常有设计思维的市场人员等等，因为那个核心信念：最具创新性的解决方案，会来自那些处在这个交叉点上的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So we've talked about all kinds of things you're amazing at. Before we transition to what you've learned about just building new stuff at larger companies, which you're very good at, can you just bullet point the skills you find you're not good at? I said we would come to this. What do you think you're not good at? And we won't go too deep here, unless you want.
turns.zh: 好。所以我们聊了各种你超厉害的事。在转到"你在更大的公司里从零打造新东西"——你非常擅长——之前，你能就把你觉得不擅长的技能列个要点吗？我说过我们会回到这。你觉得你不擅长什么？我们不会太深聊，除非你想。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So it's interesting, because I think that there are many things that we talked about that are actually a double-edged sword in practice. So, let's start with the conviction piece. I think that the good thing about being high conviction is that you're able to sell forward and to get people to feel strongly about something and a next step in the future. I think the downside of that is if there is less of a history of working together, there might be skepticism about like, "Oh, are you just pushing something because you believe in it? Or are you pushing something because our users actually needed it?" And so, in those moments, it becomes really important to constantly be highlighting user proof points.
turns.zh: 这有意思，因为我觉得我们聊的很多事，在实践中其实是把双刃剑。我们先从 conviction 这点说起。高信念感好的一面是，你能把它"卖"出去、让人们强烈感觉到某件事和未来的下一步。我觉得不好的一面是：如果一起工作的历史较短，可能会有人怀疑"哦，你推这个，只是因为你自己相信？还是因为你推这个，是因为用户真的需要它？" 所以在那些时刻，不断强调用户的证明点就变得非常重要。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think, the second is scrappiness. So, I think I have a very high ability to thrive in ambiguity and to pull things together last minute. So, for example, it's very common that I am editing a product review deck minutes before we are about to present, or that I haven't started until the night before and stay up until 3:00 AM to do it. And this is somewhat fine. But then, I think that other people don't always love it, because they're like, "Hey, maybe let's start earlier next time." I get that. The third piece would be I get very consumed by the details of something. And I think in a lot of instances, this is great. Also, at a certain point, sometimes you want to defer those decisions. And so, that's also an important skill to learn.
turns.zh: 我觉得第二是 scrappiness（将就/灵活）。我有一种在模糊中茁壮成长、并在最后一刻把东西拼起来的很强能力。比如，我常常在我们的产品评审 deck 要展示前几分钟还在改它，或者我直到前一晚才开始、熬到凌晨三点做完。这某种程度上没问题。但别人不总是喜欢，因为他们会说"嘿，也许下次我们早点开始。" 我懂。第三点是，我会非常沉浸在某件事的细节里。我觉得很多时候这很好。但到了某个点，有时你要想把那些决策 deferred（推迟）。所以这也是个重要的技能要去学。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thanks for sharing all that. This touches on something that came up in a previous podcast episode. Nikhil from Meta had this really interesting metaphor, where every superpower has a shadow. Basically, everything you're amazing at, there's something that'll be a problem, a liability basically for you. And so, I think, what you're pointing out is you're amazing at some of these things, but there's downsides. And I think that's really important for people to know. And we already talked about just something you believe that I also believe, it's just, you'll have things you're not good at, focus on things you're amazing at, and just getting better at those things, and use that to achieve, because it ends up being a lot more.
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢你分享这些。这触及了之前一期播客里出现的一个点。Meta 的 Nikhil 有个很有意思的比喻：每个超能力都有阴影。basically，你超厉害的每件事，都有个会成为问题、会成为你 liabilities（隐患）的东西。所以，你指出的是，你在一些事上超厉害，但也有 downsides。我觉得这点对人们很重要。而且我们已经聊过你相信、我也相信的一点：你会有不擅长的事，聚焦在你超厉害的事上、并把它做得更好，用它去成就，因为最终那会带来多得多。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Also, building off of that is as you scale your team, it's really important to be self-aware of what those blind spots are and to hire for that. Because, you want individuals to be spiky and you want team to be well-rounded.
turns.zh: 还有，建立在这之上的是：随着你扩展团队，对自己那些盲点有自知之明、并为此招人，非常重要。因为你想让个人有"尖峰"，也想让团队"全面均衡"。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great segue to talking about building completely new things at large companies. So, what I hear is you're the go-to person for zero-to-one stuff at Figma, which is incredible. Figma is one of the most admired, successful tech companies in the world. And, you're the person people look to build completely new stuff. So, first of all, why are you so passionate about this stuff? Why do you want to be working on brand new stuff like this? And why is it important for companies to be good at this?
turns.zh: 那是聊"在大型公司里从零打造全新东西"很好的过渡。所以我听到的是，你是 Figma 从零到一这件事的"首选人物"，这太了不起了。Figma 是世界上最受推崇、最成功的科技公司之一。而你是人们指望去 build 全新东西的人。所以首先，你为什么对这事这么热情？为什么你想做这种 brand new 的东西？为什么公司擅长这事很重要？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: In order for a company to stay competitive, a company needs to stay entrepreneurial. If you are not constantly thinking about what's next, defining the industry standard, seeing around the corner from your competitors, you will get taken over. That is a reality. And so, consequently, I personally love to screen for very entrepreneurial companies and companies that have that culture. And so, Figma has this huge run with it culture, where run with it is also one of our core values, and it's really encouraged that people can just sprint off in a direction that is seen not as a distraction, but rather a manifestation of the company's values.
turns.zh: 为了让一家公司保持竞争力，它需要保持创业精神。如果你不不断思考"下一步是什么"、定义行业标准、在竞争对手之前看穿拐角，你就会被超越。这是现实。所以相应地，我个人喜欢去筛选那些非常有创业精神、有那种文化的公司。Figma 有一个和它文化一起奔跑的 huge run（强大传统），"run with it"（放手去跑）也是我们的核心价值之一，它真的鼓励人们朝着一个方向冲刺，而这被视为不是分心，而是公司价值的体现。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so, at the company, some of our most monumental launches have come out of hackathons and have come out of bottoms up projects. So recently, this week we had a launch of Multi-edit, which was a long clamored for a feature where folks can edit things across multiple frames at the same time. That was a multi-year, multi-product long initiative. We have things like Jambot, which is an AI plugin inside of FigJam that has come out of an AI hackathon that we had last year. Our entire widgets platform was originally a hackathon project. And so, there's this culture of celebrating things-
turns.zh: 所以，在公司里，我们一些最重大的发布来自黑客马拉松、来自自下而上的项目。比如最近这周我们发布了 Multi-edit，这是一个被渴望了很久的功能，人们可以同时编辑多个画框里的东西。那是一个跨多年、跨多个产品的长倡议。我们有像 Jambot 这样的东西，它是 FigJam 里的一个 AI 插件，来自我们去年办的一场 AI 黑客马拉松。我们整个 widgets 平台 originally 就是个黑客马拉松项目。所以有这种庆祝——

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: ... project. And so there's this culture of celebrating things that have been pushed bottoms up. And so constantly thinking about how can people within the company be entrepreneurial, both in terms of getting new products up to users and in terms of improving internal processes, is just a culture that you constantly want to be facilitating and leading into.
turns.zh: ……项目的文化。所以有这种庆祝自下而上被推出来的东西的文化。所以不断思考"公司里的人怎么才能有创业精神"——既在把新产品推给用户方面，也在改善内部流程方面——是你不断想去促进和引领的文化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And clearly, Figma is very good at this. Let's dive a little deeper. Say, somebody wants to make their culture more entrepreneurial or wants to become better at this individually, maybe just broadly, what does it take to do this well, to go from idea to, "Okay, that's a huge new product for a business"? What have you learned just broadly, what are kind of the steps or the important elements of that, well?
turns.zh: 太棒了。而且显然，Figma 非常擅长这事。我们深入一点。假设有人想让自己的文化更有创业精神、或者想个人在这方面变得更好，broadly 说，把这件事做好需要什么，从想法到"好，那是业务的一个巨大新产品"？你 broadly 学到了什么，那些步骤或重要元素是什么？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think that there's this interesting metaphor that you were calling out earlier about a zero-to-one project being like a flame. And flames are interesting, because they're sort of destined to die at the end of the day. And I think about the person who is pushing a zero-to-one idea as kind of being the keeper of the flame.
turns.zh: 我觉得你之前指出过一个很有意思的比喻：一个从零到一的项目像一团火。而火很有意思，因为它们说到底注定要熄灭。我把推一个从零到一想法的人，看作那团火的守护者。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And in particular, there's this metaphor that really sticks with me, which is in Greek mythology, all the gods sit on Mount Olympus, and there's this Goddess Hestia who is the keeper of the hearth, and it is her job to always keep the hearth burning, even when all the gods peace out to go on their various quests. And I kind of think about the person or the team or the group of people who are pushing a zero-to-one idea as being the Hestias or the keepers of the hearth. And it is your job to stoke the flames and the embers if they are at risk of dying out. And it is also your job to ensure that the idea can spread like wildfire and can build that level of hype you need for an entire company or an entire set of people to be clamoring for something to get built.
turns.zh: 特别是，有一个让我印象很深的比喻：在希腊神话里，所有的神坐在奥林匹斯山上，有一位女神 Hestia，是炉灶的守护者，她的职责是始终让炉火燃烧，即使所有神都离开去各自的冒险。我有点把推一个从零到一想法的人、或团队、或一群人，看作 Hestias、炉灶的守护者。你的职责是，在火苗和余烬有熄灭风险时，去拨旺它们。你的职责也是确保这个想法能像野火一样蔓延，并建立起你需要的那种 hype，让整个公司或一整群人都轰动着想要某个东西被 build。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And so more concretely, I think that there are three things you need to do in order to be successful at bringing an idea into existence. The first is you need to have the right idea, right? And that's the empathy piece. That's the piece that you will get from having conversations day in, day out with your users. The second is you need to secure buy-in for that idea. So that's the vision piece. You need to be able to rally an entire set of folks, but honestly, most importantly, your leadership and your team behind an idea. And then, the third is you need to be able to make it spread like that wildfire. You need to get it to a point where someone joins the company and they're like, "Oh, what is that flame burning there? And how can I learn more about that?"
turns.zh: 更具体地说，我觉得要把一个想法变成现实，你需要做三件事。第一，你需要有正确的想法，对吧？那就是同理心那部分。那是从日复一日和用户对话中得到的。第二，你需要为那个想法争取到 buy-in（认同）。那就是愿景那部分。你需要能把一整群人——但老实说，最重要的是你的领导层和你的团队——团结在一个想法之后。第三，你需要能让它像野火一样蔓延。你需要把它带到这样一个点：有人加入公司，他们会像"哦，那边烧着的那团火是什么？我怎么能多了解它一点？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming up with a great idea, getting buy-in for your idea, and then spreading it within the organization, what have you learned about how to actually come up with an idea that is actually a good idea?
turns.zh: 想出一个好想法、为你的想法争取 buy-in，然后在组织内传播它——关于怎么真的想出一个"确实是好想法"的想法，你学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: So it's funny because the current product that I'm working on actually came out of a conversation or a set of conversations where I was pitching FigJam to people. And so kind of speaking about constantly having these user conversations, I think in order to have the right idea, there are two key elements. The first is you need to have that user empathy. You need to be constantly having conversations with your users, diving into what are their pain points, not only about the product that you're working on, but general perceptions about your company and also general perceptions about the other tools or products that they might be using on a daily basis. It's not enough to have a perspective on how well you are competing in the market, but you also need to know, like understand a person's full end-to-end tooling usage.
turns.zh: 这好玩，因为我正在做的这个产品，actually 来自一场或一组我在向人们 pitch FigJam 时的对话。所以说到不断有那些用户对话，我觉得要有正确的想法，有两个关键元素。第一，你需要有那种用户同理心。你需要不断和用户对话，深挖他们的痛点——不只是关于你正在做的产品，还有对你公司的整体看法、以及他们日常可能用的其他工具或产品的整体看法。光有"你在市场里竞争得多好"的视角还不够，你还需要知道，要理解一个人端到端的工具使用全貌。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then, the second thing is you need to ensure that what you're kind of working towards ladders into a company goal. And so something that's very top of mind at Figma or something that has been very top of mind at Figma has been how do we go from building for designers to covering the entire product development cycle and expanding to non-designers in particular. And non-designers is kind of this bucket term that we use for PMs and developers and marketers and so on and so forth, but how can we ensure that our tooling suite is reflective of all the different stakeholders that make the product development process what it is, and so I think that, yeah, just constantly having the conversation with the users and also constantly being anchored around not what are you currently working on, but what is the broader company goal is something that will help you come up with the right idea.
turns.zh: 然后，第二件事是，你需要确保你努力的方向，能 ladder up（逐级支撑）进一个公司目标。所以在 Figma 非常 top of mind、或曾经非常 top of mind 的一件事是：我们怎么从为设计师 build，走向覆盖整个产品开发周期、并尤其扩展到非设计师？非设计师是我们用来概括 PM、开发者、市场人员等等的一个笼统词，但我们怎么确保我们的工具套件，能反映构成产品开发过程的形形色色的利益相关者？所以我觉得，是的，不断和用户对话、也不断锚定在"不是你当前在做什么，而是更 broad 的公司目标是什么"上，会帮你想出正确的想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such an important point, basically understanding the business, not just, "Here's my feature, here's my product, or here's what feels like a great cool thing to build." Okay, so that's the idea getting buy-in. What have you learned about how to do that? Well, clearly, you've been very successful, because we've talked about a lot of these things, building hype, creating a big vision. What else there that we haven't talked about that you think is really important?
turns.zh: 这么重要的一点，basically 是理解业务，而不只是"这是我的功能、这是我的产品、或者这是感觉起来很酷值得 build 的东西。" 好，那是想法。那争取 buy-in 呢？你学到了什么去做到它？显然你非常成功，因为我们聊了很多这些——制造 hype、创造宏大愿景。还有什么我们没聊、你觉得非常重要的？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think the key to being successful at zero-to-one is to honestly have optimism that borders on delusion. You need to have insane, almost like reality distortion field where you don't hear the word no, or at the very least, you translate it into a not yet. And so I think that in terms of pitching, I'll be honest, my first few pitches of this idea were not successful. What basically happened was kind of like both conviction, the idea by talking to users, and then I would have ad hoc conversations with folks around the company, and I would be like, "We should do this." And they would be like, "Maybe." And I would be like, "Okay, what am I seeing? What are they not seeing?" And then, what basically happened was we had a PM off-site where we were talking about strategy for the next year. And I, again, pitch this, and it got kind of momentum there, but not really.
turns.zh: 我觉得在从零到一上成功的关键，是 honestly 拥有一种近乎妄想的乐观。你需要有那种疯狂的、几乎是"现实扭曲力场"，让你听不到"不"这个字，或者至少，你把它翻译成"还没"。所以说到 pitch，老实说，我对这个想法的头几次 pitch 都没成功。真正发生的是，就像一个 conviction 和想法那样——通过和用户聊，然后我会在公司里到处做 ad hoc 对话，我会说"我们应该做这个。" 他们会说"也许。" 我会说"好，我看到了什么？他们没看到什么？" 然后真正发生的是，我们有一次 PM off-site，在聊下一年的战略。我 again pitch 了这个，它在那儿有了点 momentum，但也不算真有。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then, I think the third time when it actually stuck was at the Maker Week hackathon. And this was kind of an insane experience for me, because I was actually hosting our hackathon. So I was kind of working with our VP of design, Noah, in order to spread the word about like, "Hey, everyone pitch your ideas." And to constantly, hackathons are interesting when they're virtual, right? Because you don't really know what people not in your office are doing, right? So you're constantly thinking about like, "Okay, how can you hype up the whole company, right? How can you hype up the SF office with what people are building in New York? And how can you ensure that London stays included even though there's a limited time zone overlap," and things like that. And so I was simultaneously thinking about, "Okay, how do we keep the momentum of this hackathon running? And then, also, how do I push this idea bottoms up?"
turns.zh: 然后，我觉得真正让它立住的第三次，是在 Maker Week 黑客马拉松。这对我来说是个有点疯狂的经历，因为我 actually 是那场黑客马拉松的主持人。所以我和我们的设计副总裁 Noah 一起，去传播"嘿，大家来 pitch 你们的想法。" 而不断——黑客马拉松在线上时很有意思，对吧？因为你不知道不在你办公室的人在做啥，对吧？所以你一直在想"好，你怎么给全公司 hype？怎么用纽约人在 build 的东西，给 SF 办公室 hype？又怎么确保伦敦也被 inclusion，即使时区重叠有限，" 等等。所以我同时在想"好，我们怎么保持这场黑客马拉松的 momentum？然后，我又怎么自下而上推这个想法？"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And I think that something that's really important when you're making a pitch is to not be daunted by the scale of your pitch. So, for example, in this instance, the proposal was basically to introduce a new product. And building a product in a week is for all intents and purposes kind of crazy, but this is I think where the scrappiness piece comes in. You need to be willing to be very clear about where you're willing to take the hit on quality or believability and where you need to push in order to make your thing feel believable. So one example of something that we did was we literally, in order to make this new product feel more real, and this was maybe a two line change in code, was we swapped out the FigJam icon in our file browser to this new icon.
turns.zh: 我觉得在做一个 pitch 时非常重要的一点，是不要被你 pitch 的规模吓倒。比如，在这个例子里，提案基本上是要引入一个新产品。而一周内 build 一个产品，就所有意图和目的来说，有点疯狂，但我觉得这就是 scrappiness 那部分派上用场的地方。你需要愿意非常清楚：你愿意在哪些地方承受质量或可信度上的打击、又需要在哪些地方推进、让你的东西显得可信。比如我们做的一件事：我们 literally，为了让这个新产品显得更真实——而这大概只是代码里两行的改动——把文件浏览器里 FigJam 的图标，换成了这个新图标。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And adding a whole new entry point is a lot of work, and you can't do that. But just swapping something and taking about what exists and changing the minor things in order to communicate what is different about your idea versus what exists today is something that you really want to lean into. And what basically happened was that at the end of the week, we had this demo day, and I was going between introducing each of the demos to doing the demo and did a little wardrobe change in between. And I think that what ended up being really great about presenting an idea like this in a company-wide forum, which I highly recommend, is that at that point, it becomes not just you evangelizing the idea, but your teammates and your colleagues and your peers evangelizing the idea. And that sense of momentum carries a lot of weight, I think.
turns.zh: 而加一个全新的入口是个大工程，你做不了。但只是换掉已有的东西、改动那些小地方，去传达"你的想法和今天已有的东西有什么不同"，是你真的要依靠的。真正发生的是，在那周结束时，我们有了 demo day，我在介绍每个 demo 和做 demo 之间来回切换，中间还换了套衣服。我觉得，在公司范围的论坛上呈现这样一个想法——我强烈推荐——真正很棒的地方在于：到了那个点，它不再只是你在传福音，而是你的队友、同事、同侪都在传福音。而那种 momentum 承载了很大的分量，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this kind of leads into the next bullet point you shared of spreading the idea across the company. It feels like this is part of it just getting it spread in a big powerful way initially. But what else have you learned about just getting this to spread across the company? It gets kind of like this flame spreading throughout the organization.
turns.zh: 这 kind of 引向你分享的下一个要点：在公司里传播这个想法。感觉这部分就是最初就让它以一种强大有力方式传播开。但关于怎么让它在公司里传播，你还学到了什么？它就像一团火在整个组织里蔓延。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think something that's very unique about Figma as compared to other companies is we have a multi-month plus long staging or dogfooding process. And so something that was really interesting to me was... One of the first projects that I worked on at the company was we were building sections inside of FigJam. And we had a problem. We built it. We put something on staging, and I was kind of like, "Okay, cool, it's been on staging a week, now we can launch, right?" And I was greeted with like, "No, we can't launch."
turns.zh: 我觉得 Figma 和其他公司非常不同的一点，是我们有一个长达数月以上的 staging（预发布）或 dogfooding（内部试用）过程。所以有件让我很感兴趣的事是…… 我在公司的第一个项目，我们在 FigJam 里 build sections。我们有个问题。我们 build 好了。我们把它放到了 staging 上，我就像"好，酷，它在 staging 上一周了，现在我们可以发布了，对吧？" 然后人家告诉我"不，我们不能发布。"

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And I think that leaning into that willingness to being vulnerable about your product and this acknowledgement that feedback is a gift, and that bits and pieces of feedback from across the company will help your product mature and get to a place where it's ready to go out the door is really important. And what's really interesting is this helps the team who's working on the product, because you're getting feedback, and that's the most direct benefit of putting something on staging early.
turns.zh: 我觉得，依靠那种愿意在你的产品上暴露弱点（vulnerable）、以及那种"反馈是礼物"的认知，并承认来自全公司的点点滴滴反馈，会帮助你的产品成熟、到达可以出门的状态，这非常重要。而很有意思的是，这帮到了做这个产品的团队，因为你得到了反馈，而那是把东西早早放到 staging 上最直接的好处。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: But the other benefit about putting something on staging early is that it makes people invested in your product. So if you think about why are betas so valuable and why are alphas so valuable, it's because when someone gives you feedback, and then the team in charge implements that change, you see that and you're like, "I shaped that part of the product." Right? And to the extent that you can get as many people in the company feeling like they shaped X, Y, Z parts of the product, I think that's really powerful, because, then, you kind of are ensuring that there's this constant feedback loop, and there's this constant investment in thinking about how can we collectively drive towards success, because at the end of the day, product development is a team sport, right? It takes everyone to make something successful. And so I just think about putting things early on staging and getting people involved in the cycle as opening up the doors to the product development process, and hopefully, that just elevates the quality of the product.
turns.zh: 但早早把东西放到 staging 上的另一个好处是，它让人们对你的产品有了投入感。所以如果你想想，为什么 beta 这么有价值、为什么 alpha 这么有价值——是因为当有人给了你反馈，然后负责的团队实现了那个改变，你看到那个，你会像"我塑造了产品的那部分。" 对吧？在你能让公司里尽可能多的人觉得他们塑造了产品的 X、Y、Z 部分的程度上，我觉得那非常有力，因为然后你 basically 确保了有这么一个持续的反馈回路、有这么一种持续的对"我们怎么集体推动走向成功"的思考，因为归根结底，产品开发是项团队运动，对吧？它需要所有人去让某件事成功。所以我觉得，把东西早早放到 staging 上、让人们卷入这个周期，就是向产品开发过程敞开大门，而希望那能提升产品的质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you want to touch on or share or leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电轮之前，还有什么你想触碰、分享、或留给听众的吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: If you have an insight that only you have, I think on one hand, you can kind of believe, "Oh, other people aren't thinking similar to me. Therefore, maybe, I'm wrong," but I would actually flip that, because I think if you have an insight that other people are not seeing, it is even more on you to get people onto the same page. And so to the extent that you can shout from the rooftops about all the insights that you're learning, I think that, in and of itself, creates a more entrepreneurial culture within the company, because chances are other people will see you doing that. They'll be inspired to contribute in the same way as well.
turns.zh: 如果你有一个只有你才有的洞察，我觉得一方面，你可能会想"哦，别人不和我想的一样。所以也许，我错了"，但我反而会翻转它，因为我觉得，如果你有一个别人没看到的洞察，那就更该由你去让大家站在同一页上。所以，在你能够就你学到的所有洞察"从屋顶大声喊"的程度上，我觉得那本身就在公司内部创造了一种更有创业精神的文化，因为很可能别人会看到你这么做。他们也会受启发，以同样的方式去贡献。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think the last thing that I would say is, which is maybe an aspect that we did not touch on, is that understanding motivations is, in my opinion, one of the keys to running a team successfully and driving an idea forward. So, for example, if you think about the composition of a product team, you have engineers, you have designers, you have researchers, data scientists, et cetera, and different people want to be involved in the kind of product visioning phase to a different extent. There's some people who do want a solution handed to them, because for them, the most exciting part of the process is to find the technical solution in the code. On the other hand, there are other people who find it really hard to feel passionately about a thing that they have not contributed to. And so I think to the extent that you can understand these motivations of your team, of your leadership, of your peers, and constantly ensure that you are catering to the individual, as opposed to the average, that is what, in my opinion, leads to one of the highest-functioning teams.
turns.zh: 我觉得我要说的最后一件事，可能是我们没触碰的一个方面：理解动机，在我看来，是成功运作一个团队、并推动一个想法向前的钥匙之一。比如，如果你想想一个产品团队的构成，你有工程师、设计师、研究员、数据科学家等等，不同的人想要参与到"产品愿景阶段"的程度是不同的。有些人确实想要一个被交到手上的解决方案，因为对他们来说，过程中最兴奋的部分，是在代码里找到技术解决方案。另一方面，也有些人很难对他们没贡献过的东西产生热情。所以我觉得，在你能够理解你的团队、你的领导层、你的同侪的这些动机，并不断确保你是在 catering to（迎合）个体、而不是平均值的程度上，那在我看来，才会带来最高效能的团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a cool point. It comes back to the personality tests that you spoke of earlier. Is that the best way to figure this out? Is it more just watch people and try to guess at what they're most excited about [inaudible 01:31:21]-
turns.zh: 这么酷的一点。它回到了你早先说的性格测试。那是搞清楚这个最好的方式吗？还是更多只是观察人、去猜他们最兴奋什么 [inaudible 01:31:21]——

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Oh, I think you have to directly ask them. So anytime someone joins my team, especially on the engineering side, because I think this is where there's the greatest variance, I will literally ask, " How much do you like being involved in product decisions?" And to the extent that you can take decisions in the open, that is excellent. And even if the decision is something along the lines of like, "Okay, we have four options," and you can go in with a leading point of view, but giving everyone the opportunity to voice their perspective and push back, if they want to, I think that that's very powerful.
turns.zh: 哦，我觉得你必须直接问他们。所以任何时候有人加入我的团队，尤其是工程侧，因为我觉得这里方差最大，我会 literally 问"你有多喜欢参与产品决策？" 而在你能公开地做决策时，那就 excellent。即使决策类似"好，我们有四个选项"，你可以带着一个主导观点进去，但给每个人机会去表达他们的视角、并在想 push back 时 push back，我觉得那非常有力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good tip. I feel like I could ask you questions for at least two more hours, but we're not going to do that. Maybe, we'll have round two some day. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 这么好的一条建议。我觉得我还能再问你至少两个小时的问题，但我们不这么干。也许，将来会有 round two。话虽如此，我们到了非常激动人心的闪电轮。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I am ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mihika, first question, what are two or three books that you recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: Mahika，第一个问题，你会最常推荐给别人的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, I'll start by saying that I am immediately skeptical of anyone who has not read Harry Potter. So, if you're one of those people, go read Harry Potter. Maybe, it contributes to creativity. I don't know.
turns.zh: 对，我先说，我对任何没读过 Harry Potter 的人都立刻持怀疑态度。所以，如果你是那些人之一，去读 Harry Potter。maybe 它有助于创造力。我不知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Now, we're talking about every book in the series, or at least the one book?
turns.zh: 现在，我们说的是系列里的每一本，还是至少那一本书？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: No, no. You have to read the entire series, and you have to read it in order. It's actually funny, when I was in kindergarten, my mom bought the fifth book, and then the person at the bookstore was like, "No, no." Like, "No, no." We were like, "Okay, got it." And then, the others that I would recommend are from a fiction perspective. I think Pachinko by Min Jin Lee is incredibly beautiful and powerful. It's like a multi-generational Korean saga. I think I'm personally just motivated and moved by large scale things. So to see a single story traverse so many generations was very fascinating to me.
turns.zh: 不，不。你得读整个系列，而且得按顺序读。好玩的是，我上幼儿园时，我妈买了第五本，然后书店的人说"不，不。" 像"不，不。" 我们就像"好，明白了。" 然后，我会推荐的其他书，从小说角度，我觉得 Min Jin Lee 的《Pachinko》（柏青哥）极其优美而有力。它像是一个跨代韩国家族传奇。我个人就是被大规模的东西激励和打动。所以看到一个单一故事穿越这么多代，让我很着迷。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then, from a more businessy book perspective, which is maybe more what you're getting at, I think that I honestly pseudo steer clear of how-to books, but one that has had a particularly large impact on me is Creativity Inc. by Ed Catmull. And this is about the founding story and scaling of Pixar. And what was so interesting to me about this book was it basically talks about how you create a process around cultivating creativity. And it's interesting, because creativity is so unencumbered and process is the opposite, so that's very fascinating.
turns.zh: 然后，从更偏商业的书的角度——也许更是你想问的——我 honestly 有点避开那些 how-to 书，但有一本对我影响特别大的，是 Ed Catmull 的《Creativity Inc.》（创新公司）。这是关于皮克斯的创立故事和规模化。这本书让我觉得最有趣的是，它 basically 讲的是你怎么围绕培养创造力，去创建一个流程。这很有意思，因为创造力是如此不受拘束，而流程正相反，所以那非常引人入胜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My favorite lesson from that book is that it sticks with me as the ugly baby metaphor, which feels like so tied to the way you think and operate. And I won't get into it. By the way, have you read The Overstory?
turns.zh: 我从那本书里最喜欢的教训，是那个一直留在我心里的"丑宝宝"（ugly baby）比喻，它感觉和你思考、运作的方式如此相系。我就不展开讲了。顺便，你读过《The Overstory》（树冠上）吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I have not. I'll add that to my list.
turns.zh: 我没读过。我会把它加到我的清单上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like, based on the way you described Pachinko, this is a book for you. It's a multi-generational family story that I did not actually finish. It's very long, but I feel like you were there.
turns.zh: 我觉得，基于你描述《Pachinko》的方式，这是本给你的书。它是一个跨代家族故事，我 actually 没读完。它很长，但我觉得你就像身临其境。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There you go.
turns.zh: 给你。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I'll go order it.
turns.zh: 我去下单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 好。最近最喜欢的电影或剧集？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Favorite recent TV show would definitely be Severance.
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的剧集，绝对是《Severance》（人生切割术）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Movie, or shall we move on?
turns.zh: 电影呢，还是我们继续？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Oh, movie, I recently watched Dune 2 and Dune 1 in the span of a week. It was really fun. I watched Dune 2, because someone asked me to co-host a premiere of Dune 2 with them, and I was like, "Okay, sounds good, sounds cool, but I need to watch Dune 1."
turns.zh: 哦，电影，我最近一周内连看了《Dune 2》和《Dune 1》。真的好玩。我看《Dune 2》是因为有人让我和他们一起主持《Dune 2》的首映，我就想"好，听起来不错，听起来酷，但我得先看《Dune 1》。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good choice. I just watched Dune 2. I don't know if a more epic movie can be made. I was just gripped.
turns.zh: 好选择。我刚看了《Dune 2》。我不知道还能不能拍出更史诗的电影。我完全被抓住了。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: The visuals were stunning.
turns.zh: 视觉效果太惊艳了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like not breathing.
turns.zh: 像没在呼吸。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's out of control. I watched it IMAX. I think that was a good call, but it was stressful. Favorite interview question they like to ask folks when you're hiring.
turns.zh: 失控了。我看的是 IMAX。我觉得那是个好决定，但挺紧张的。你招聘时喜欢问的最喜欢的面试问题？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I like to ask people what motivates them, but also, people often ask me, what is my favorite hot seat question, which I think is kind of similar. And my answer to that is that it's highly dependent on the person, and there's no go-to hot seat question. And I almost feel the same way about interview questions.
turns.zh: 我喜欢问人们什么在激励他们，但人们也常问我，我最喜欢的 hot seat 问题是什么，我觉得那有点类似。而我对那个的回答是，它高度取决于人，并没有什么 go-to 的 hot seat 问题。而我对面试问题也几乎是同样的感觉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite product you recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 你最近发现、并爱上的最喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Speaking about hype, I am kind of obsessed with the browser company, Arc onboarding flow, specifically the onboarding flow. I think that they do such a good job of amping you up for not only the larger change that they're trying to make in terms of personal operating system, but of showing you to what extent their team thinks about the details of the product, where a lot of other products might cut corners. And I think their ability to communicate the ethos of their product through that is really powerful. So that's one.
turns.zh: 说到 hype，我有点迷恋浏览器公司 Arc 的 onboarding 流程，具体说是那个 onboarding 流程。我觉得他们做得太好了——不仅为他们在"个人操作系统"上试图做出的更大改变把你点燃，还向你展示了他们的团队在思考产品细节上到了什么程度，而很多其他产品可能会偷工减料。我觉得他们通过那个流程传达产品精神（ethos）的能力，真的很强。所以这是其一。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: And then I think the second is in the AI space. I'm really excited by Pika, which is video generation, video editing software. I think that, in my mind, one of the biggest shortcomings of AI, the way that a lot of people are building it today is that it's optimized for the demo or optimized for the tweet, right? And it's basically this situation where I think about it as, in my mind, one of the biggest goals of AI right now is the black boxification of AI, because it's not really useful to enter a prompt and get an output that you can't interact with, because then it's like, if something's a little bit off, what are you going to do? You're kind of stuck. But I think Pika is doing a really great job of not just investing in the foundational video models, but also giving you the ability to manipulate the output. And so I'm excited about that approach, and I hope that more companies take you from that.
turns.zh: 然后我觉得第二是 AI 领域的。我对 Pika 很兴奋，它是视频生成、视频编辑软件。我觉得，在我心里，今天很多人构建 AI 的方式，最大的短板之一是它为 demo 优化、或为 tweet 优化，对吧？而基本上就是这种情况：我觉得，当前 AI 最大的目标之一，是 AI 的"黑箱化"（black boxification），因为输入一个 prompt、得到一个你没法交互的输出，其实没多大用，因为如果有点偏差，你怎么办？你 basically 卡住了。但我觉得 Pika 做得很好的一点，是不只投资基础的视频模型，也给你操控输出的能力。所以我对那种方式很兴奋，也希望更多公司从那出发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, good choices on Arc. Whenever anyone ask me for a great onboarding follow, that's the one I point people to. And we had Josh Miller on the podcast in the past, and I was proud that he pinned our interview as top of his Twitter feed for a year, which made me really happy. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to or share with friends or family that you find useful in life or in work?
turns.zh: 太棒了，Arc 选得好。每当有人问我有什么好的 onboarding 推荐，我指的就是那个。我们之前请过 Josh Miller 上播客，我很骄傲他把我们的访谈置顶在他的 Twitter 动态一年，那让我很开心。你有什么喜欢的、会常常回到它、或分享给朋友家人的人生格言吗，你觉得在生活或工作中有用？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, "Life is a game of expectations." And so speaking of books and movies and things like that, I will never ever watch a movie trailer or read the back cover of a book, because I think it means that you're going into it with too many expectations. It either tells you all the punchlines, or it tells you the foundational backstory or something like that. And I think that, to the extent, that you go in either with no expectations or low expectations, that's the key to enjoying life.
turns.zh: 有，"Life is a game of expectations."（生活是一场关于期待的游戏。） 所以说到书、电影和这类东西，我永远、永远不会看电影预告片、或读书的封底，因为我觉得那意味着你带着太多期待进去。它要么把所有的笑点都告诉你，要么把基础背景故事之类告诉你。而我觉得，在你带着零期待或低期待进去的程度上，才是享受生活的关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that tip. I recently learned the same piece of advice from Kevin Kelly's recent book where it's just a book of little tidbits of advice that he's learned over his life, and one of them is like never watch the trailer if you're going to watch the movie, and I've been doing that ever since. I think that's an awesome piece of advice. Final question. We talked about the Figgy's. You mentioned there's an award for PM least likely to write a PRD. Was that you won the award for chance?
turns.zh: 我爱这条建议。我最近从 Kevin Kelly 的新书里学到了同样的建议，那本书就是他一生学到的小建议集，其中一条就是"如果你要去看电影，永远别看预告片"，我从那以后一直这么做。我觉得那是个超棒的建议。最后一个问题。我们聊了 Figgies。你提到有个"最不可能写 PRD 的 PM"奖。那是你碰巧得奖了吗？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I think it was me and Sho tied.
turns.zh: 我觉得是我和 Sho 并列。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great. I guessed correctly. Amazing. Mihika, you're... Everything, I hope you'd be on this podcast, I feel like, we could have talked for, I keep saying this, but at least two more hours maybe, we'll have a follow-up.
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。我猜对了。太了不起了。Mahika，你——所有事，我希望你上这个播客，我觉得，我们本可以聊——我一直在说这个——但至少还能再聊两小时 maybe，我们会有个后续。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: I'd love that.
turns.zh: 我很乐意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you so much for being here and for making time. Two final questions. Where can folks find you if they want to reach out and follow up on anything? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 非常感谢你来到这里、并抽出时间。最后两个问题。大家想联系你、跟进任何事的话，去哪里找你？听众怎么帮你忙？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Yeah, you can find me on Twitter. I'm @mihikapoor. It's kind of my first name and last name smushed together. And in terms of how users can be useful to me, so one is come to Config, we will be announcing both this new product, but also so many cool things that the company is working on. A lot of very exciting AI launches and more. And I think that having the community come together is a very special moment. So hope to see you there. Cough, cough, try the new product when it comes out. And I don't know, I'm always on the lookout for cool new products. I like to be someone who tries things out early, so to the extent that you see things, send them my way.
turns.zh: 对，你可以在 Twitter 上找到我。我是 @mihikapoor。基本上是我的名和姓拼在一起。至于用户怎么对我有用，一是来 Config，我们会宣布这款新产品，也会宣布公司正在做的很多很酷的事。很多非常令人兴奋的 AI 发布等等。我觉得让社区聚到一起，是个非常特别的时刻。所以希望在那见到你。咳咳，新产品出来时试试它。而且我不知道，我一直在留意很酷的新产品。我喜欢做那个早早试用东西的人，所以只要你看到东西，发给我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's going to be so many people anticipating this new product.
turns.zh: 会有超多人期待这款新产品。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Oh, no, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，不，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's going to be like-
turns.zh: 会有像——

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: We should-
turns.zh: 我们应该——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... holy moly.
turns.zh: ……我的天。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Please have low expectations.
turns.zh: 请保持低期待。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And the way we'll know is are you pitching and presenting it, or how do we know this is going to be your product once we see it?
turns.zh: 好。而我们怎么知道呢，是你来 pitch 和呈现它，还是我们怎么知道这会是你的产品、一旦我们看到它？

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: It'll probably be in the opening keynote, which is done by Dylan, but I'll probably give a Config talk on it as well. So that's how you will know, and I'll probably tweet about it. What I was actually going to do is to release the original vision deck when it launches, so you can look out for that.
turns.zh: 它可能会在开幕主题演讲里，那是 Dylan 做的，但我可能也会就它做一场 Config 演讲。所以那是我们怎么知道的方式，而且我可能会发 tweet。我 actually 打算做的是，在它发布时放出原始的愿景 deck，所以你可以留意那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We'll be watching. I will be at Config.
turns.zh: 我们会关注。我会去 Config。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Can't wait to see you there.
turns.zh: 等不及在那见到你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Potentially on stage. Can't reveal yet what's happening exactly, but I think it's going to be awesome. Anyway, Mihika, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 可能在台上。我还不能透露具体会发生什么，但我觉得会超棒。总之，Mahika，再次非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Mihika Kapoor
turns.en: Thank you for having me, Lenny. This was such a fun conversation. It was such an honor and a privilege to be on the podcast. So, really, thank you so much for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，Lenny。这对话太好玩了。能上这个播客是我的荣幸和特权。所以，真的非常感谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The honor was mine. Bye, everyone. Thank you so much for listening. turns.zh: 荣幸是我的。再见，大家。非常感谢收听。如果你觉得这有价值，你可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或你喜欢的播客应用上订阅这个节目。另外，请考虑给我们打分或留评论，因为那真的能帮其他听众找到这个播客。你可以在 lennyspodcast.com 找到所有往期节目或了解更多关于节目的信息。下期见。
